Delcassé and France's Break with the Vatican.

In his newly published memoirs, which bring to light fresh material in the "Revue de Paris," concerning France's greatest Foreign Minister Deleassé, Octave Homberg states that Delcassé had been opposed to France's break with the Vatican at the time. Although a Radical Socialist, he was not anticlerical; as Foreign Minister, he had moreover come to appreciate the moral power of the Papacy. He did everything to prevent Combes from breaking the Concordat. The President of the Republic, who alone was kept informed, dispatched Victor Homberg on a secret mission to Rome without the knowledge of the French embassy there, in order to obtain concessions, particularly regarding the appointment of bishops, through the mediation of Cardinal Rampolla; these concessions were intended to enable President Loubet, Delcassé, and two other ministers to oppose the rupture of the Concordat within the Cabinet. M. Homberg did indeed bring back certain modifications to the Concordat from Rome. However, the anticlerical passion of Combes was stronger, and in a stormy cabinet meeting, the break was decided.

Europäische Wiederaufbau-
Bedingungen
Washington, 4. Mai. Der
stellvertretende Arbeitsminister David Morse
legte in einer Pressekonferenz gestern
einen Bericht vor, den Philip Kaiser,
Leiter der Abteilung für internationale
Angelegenheiten im Arbeitsministerium,
über die Arbeitsverhältnisse in Europa
verfaßt hat. Kaiser, der mehrere Monate
zu Studienzwecken in Europa verbrachte,
trifft in seinem Bericht die Feststellung,
daß nach allgemeiner Auffassung der
zuständigen europäischen Stellen die
höchstmögliche Steigerung der
Produktion wichtiger als Hilfsmaßnahmen sei,
um Europa wieder auf eigene Füße zu
stellen. Vollproduktion sei der einzige
Weg, der Aussichten auf eine wirkliche
europäische Wiedergesundung eröffne..
In dem Bericht Kaisers wird weiter
ausgeführt, daß die aufbauwillige
europäische Arbeiterschaft noch „unter dem
Druck aktiver Gegenkräfte" stehe, die
den Marshall-Plan bekämpften, und daß
die europäischen Arbeiter selbst „eine
wichtige Rolle bei dem Gelingen oder
dem Scheitern des Wiederaufbaus von
Europa spielen werden."
Morse erklärte, da s
Arbeitsministerium sei an einem Ausbau der
wechselseitigen Handelabkommen durch den
Kongreß interessiert. Die Verhandlungen
mit anderen Nationen im Rahmen des
hierfür erlassenen Gesetzes seien eng mit
der Verwirklichung des - europäischen
Wiederaufbauprogramms verknüpft. Auf
diese Weise würden die Vorteile, die
sich aus dem europäischen
Wiederaufbauprogramm ergeben, den Farmern,
Arbeitern und Geschäftsleuten der
Vereinigten Staaten ebenso zugute kommen
wie denjenigen Europas.

European Reconstruction Conditions

Washington, May 4. Deputy Labor Secretary David Morse presented a report at a press conference yesterday, prepared by Philip Kaiser, head of the International Affairs Division of the Labor Department, on labor conditions in Europe. Kaiser, who spent several months in Europe for study purposes, states in his report that, according to the general view of the relevant European authorities, the greatest possible increase in production is more important than aid measures in order to put Europe back on its own feet. Full production is the only path that offers prospects for a genuine European recovery.

Kaiser’s report further explains that the reconstruction-willing European workforce is still “under the pressure of active opposing forces” that are fighting the Marshall Plan, and that European workers themselves “will play an important role in the success or failure of Europe’s reconstruction.”

Morse stated that the Labor Department is interested in expanding reciprocal trade agreements through Congress. Negotiations with other nations under the law enacted for this purpose are closely linked to the implementation of the European reconstruction program. In this way, the benefits arising from the European reconstruction program will accrue to the farmers, workers, and businesspeople of the United States just as much as to those of Europe.

12 Stürmer schießen ein Goal
Es ist beschämend, zwölf
österreichische Stürmer, die im A und B-Team
gegen die Tschechoslowakei in Wien
und Bratislava antraten, schössen nur
einen Treffer, und der Mann, der dieses
Kunststück zuwege brachte, ist der
Nestor dieses Dutzend, der 35jährige
Pepi Stroh von der Wiener Austria. Es
waren nicht zehn sondern zwölf
Stürmer, da je ein Mann in beiden
Mannschaften in der Pause ausgetauscht
wurde.
War bisher die Stürmerreihe das
Sorgenkind des Verbandskapitäns, ist
es nun die Halfreihe geworden, denn
außer dem Mittelläufer Gewirk von der
Austria zeigten seine beiden Helfer
nicht viel erfreuliches. Lediglich der
Tormann und die Verteidigung
konnten befriedigen. Während die
österreichische Nationalmannschaft in
Bratislava 3 —1 besiegt wurde, unterlag
das österreichische B-Team in Wien
bei strömendem Regen vor nur 35 000
Zuschauern 1—0.
Der einzige Hoffnungsstrahl in
diesem Unglück war das Wiener
Jugendteam, das gegen die slovakische Jugend
in Bratislava antrat, ganz
ausgezeichnet spielte und 3—1 gewann.
Und noch ein Länderkampf ging
verlor
en. Auch die Tischtennisspieler führten
einen Länderkampf durch. Die Ungarn
waren in Wien zu Gast und setzten
ihre Siegesserie — seit zehn Jahren
hat Oesterreich noch keinen
Länderkampf gegen Ungarn gewonnen — fort.
5—1 wurde Oesterreich geschlagen u.
auch bei den anschließenden
internationalen Meisterschaften kamen die
Gäste aus der CSR und Ungarn zu
Siegen. Den einzigen Punkt für
Oesterreich erzielte Just, der den besten
Ungarn Sido schlagen kannte.
Die ehemalige Weltmeisterin Pritzi,
die heuer einen Monat in Luxemburg
weilte, verlor knapp 3—2 gegen die
ausgezeichnete Ungarin Farkas.

Der Güttinger Mord vor dem Schwurgericht.
Der Fall liegt weit zurück, mehr denn ein Jahr.
Im Schloß Güttingen lebte ein Sonderling, der
Berner Albert Rätzer, der ein arbeitreiches Leben als
Privatier beschließen wollte, in Wirklichkeit sich aber den
Lebensabend durch allerlei eingebildete Schikanen ver
bitterte. Diesen Rätzer fand sein Dienstpersonal am Nach
mittag des 11. Septembers 1907 im Treppenhaus in
den letzten Zügen liegend; ein Fremder erklärte, Rätzer
wäre die Stiege hinuntergestürzt; man lief dahin, dort
hin, während der Schloßherr, ohne je zur Besinnung zu
kommen, den Geist aufgab. Dem Arzt fiel es nicht
schwer, zu konstatieren, daß etwas Ungewöhnliches vor
gefallen war; erst jetzt fielen dem Dienstpersonal allerlei
Nebenumstände ein; jetzt erst ward jeder davon über
zeugt, daß Rätzer einem Mordanschlag zum Opfer ge
fallen war.
Wer waren die Täter? Am 6. September hatte ein
Dr. Meier vorgesprochen, der das Schloß kaufen wollte.
Am 9. war ein Fräulein Josephine Zapf erschienen, die
so gut Wetter zu machen verstand, daß man sie gegen
alle Gewohnheit bis zum verhängnisvollen Mittwoch den
11. September beherbergte. Da war Dr. Meier wieder
gekommen. Und wieder hatte ihm Rätzer sein Besitztum
gezeigt. Dabei war der Schloßbesitzer „verunglückt":
Dr. Meier und Fräulein Zapf aber waren spurlos ver
schwunden.
In einer Villa in Thielle, Kanton Neuenburg, lebte
ein Dr. Meier mit seiner Mutter Witwe Meier und einer
Haushälterin Josephine Zapf. Die Leute waren im
März 1907 gekommen. Bald blieb der, bald der andere
Lieferant unbezahlt: so ward es nachgerade wohlbekannt,
daß die Leute wenig Geld besaßen. Da, am 13. Sep
tember, konnte Meier Zahlungen im Betrage von 1500
Fr. leisten. Das fiel auf. Und am Abend gleichen Ta
ges saßen Dr. Meier und die Zapf bereits hinter Schloß
und Riegel.
Da sich die Leute im Schlosse Güttingen um ihren
Herrn bemühten, hatte Meier am Geldschrank operiert
und ihm verschiedene Wertpapiere, Obligationen der
Thurgauischen Hypothekenbank, eine auf den Namen
lautende Obligation der Stadt Konstanz, sowie unge
fähr 1700 Fr. in bar entnommen. Dann waren Meier
und die Zapf nach Zürich gefahren, wo sie im Hotel
„Bellevue" abstiegen. Den folgenden Morgen benützte
die Zapf dazu, um die Obligationen der Thurgauischen
Hypothekenbank zu versilbern; darauf reiste das Paar
nach Thielle ab, doch nur, um schon folgenden Tages
dem Häscher in die Hände zu fallen. Rätzer hatte zu
gut Buch geführt, als daß nicht der genaue Werttitel
bestand hätte ermittelt werden können.
Wer war dieser Dr. Meier, der sich als Zahnarzt
ausgegeben hatte? Es stellte sich bald heraus, daß Be
ruf und Titel seinem bereits verstorbenen Vater, der in
Zürich praktiziert hatte, entliehen worden waren. Meier
selber war weder Zahnarzt noch Doktor, nichts mehr
nichts weniger denn ein Vagant, der seit 1904 nach
einander in Verona, in Tettnang, in Mogelsberg, in
der Villa Tigelsberg, in Berneck, in Thielle seinen
Wohnsitz aufgeschlagen hatte und überall desselben

completion:
The Güttingen Murder Before the Jury Court.

The case dates far back, more than a year ago. In Güttingen Castle lived an eccentric, the Bernese Albert Rätzer, who wished to conclude a life of hard work as a private citizen, but in reality had embittered his final years through all sorts of imagined harassments. This Rätzer was found by his domestic staff on the afternoon of September 11, 1907, lying in the stairwell in his final moments; a stranger stated that Rätzer had fallen down the stairs; people ran here and there, while the castle's master, without ever regaining consciousness, breathed his last. It was not difficult for the doctor to determine that something unusual had occurred; only now did the domestic staff recall various incidental circumstances; only now was everyone convinced that Rätzer had fallen victim to a murderous attack.

Who were the perpetrators? On September 6, a Dr. Meier had called, wanting to buy the castle. On the 9th, a Miss Josephine Zapf had appeared, who understood so well how to ingratiate herself that, contrary to all custom, she was accommodated until the fateful Wednesday, September 11. Then Dr. Meier had come again. And once more, Rätzer had shown him his property. During this, the castle owner had "had an accident": but Dr. Meier and Miss Zapf had disappeared without a trace.

In a villa in Thielle, Canton of Neuchâtel, lived a Dr. Meier with his mother, the widow Meier, and a housekeeper, Josephine Zapf. The people had arrived in March 1907. Soon one supplier, then another, remained unpaid: thus it gradually became well-known that these people had little money. Then, on September 13, Meier was able to make payments amounting to 1,500 francs. This attracted attention. And on the evening of the same day, Dr. Meier and Zapf were already behind lock and key.

While the people in Güttingen Castle were occupied with their master, Meier had operated on the safe and taken from it various securities, bonds of the Thurgau Mortgage Bank, a bond issued in the name of the City of Constance, as well as approximately 1,700 francs in cash. Then Meier and Zapf traveled to Zurich, where they stayed at the "Bellevue" hotel. The following morning, Zapf used the time to cash the bonds of the Thurgau Mortgage Bank; thereafter the pair departed for Thielle, but only to fall into the hands of the law the very next day. Rätzer had kept his books too well for the exact securities not to have been able to be identified.

Who was this Dr. Meier, who had presented himself as a dentist? It soon emerged that both profession and title had been borrowed from his already deceased father, who had practiced in Zurich. Meier himself was neither a dentist nor a doctor, nothing more and nothing less than a vagrant, who since 1904 had successively taken up residence in Verona, in Tettnang, in Mogelsberg, in the Villa Tigelsberg, in Berneck, in Thielle, and everywhere enjoyed the same reputation as a bad payer. Zapf? A Württemberg native, with whom Meier had lodged in Tettnang, who often lived with Meier, only to separate from him when circumstances required; as in June 1907, when she had entered service with a family in Zurich. Zapf was a woman approaching forty, Meier only twenty-eight.

Exactly eight days after the murder in Güttingen Castle, Meier and Zapf were extradited to the Thurgau authorities. The investigation began; it brought to light for Zapf a history of theft, which will also make her acquainted with the Zurich jury. Zapf proved to the examining magistrate to be an astonishing teller of fairy tales. But by this time, the murderer and his accomplice had already receded into the background of public interest due to the intervening publication of the victim's will, that of Albert Rätzer, which testament was presented quite extensively in No. 271, in the second morning edition. In this last will and testament, Rätzer revealed himself as the pronounced quarrelsome nature that he was. One certainly still remembers the formulation of the will, downright insulting to the Canton of Thurgau, according to which the Federal Council was appointed the main heir of the estate, then estimated at roughly 300,000 francs.

Then it gradually grew quiet. One still heard how the house search in Thielle had brought to light quite incriminating material. Then Meier's name was linked to the death of a young man in Berneck. The investigation dragged on. Finally, it could be concluded: it ended with the summons of Meier and Zapf before the jury court in Weinfelden.

original_text:
Der Rückblick auf das Jahr 1827, welchen das Appenzellische Mo
natsblatt, für Appenzell-Außerrhoden entworfen hat, schließt sich
mit folgender Stelle: „Zwey wichtige Gegenstände und die vollgültigsten
Zeugen für die fortschreitende Aufklärung fallen in der Geschichte des
verflossenen Jahres besonders auf: der Eifer für den Jugendunterricht
und die Oeffentlichkeit in allgemeinen Angelegenheiten. Nicht nur nimmt.
die Zahl der öffentlichen Schulen täglich zu, auch Privatschulen, die
zum Theil jene noch übertreffen, mehren sich täglich. Immer vorherr
schender wird besonders die Liebe zum Gesang, Der große Sängerver
ein hat eine Menge Filiale, wo Jung und Alt, Männer und Frauen
die Gesangübungen fleißig und eifrig besuchen. — Mit Gewinn und
Gewerb steht es wenigstens nicht schlechter als vor einem Jahre; eher
etwas besser. Nirgends ist Mangel an Arbeit, und so viel wie die Le
bensmittel, mögen auch die Arbeitslöhne gestiegen seyn. Drückenden
Mangel leidet Niemand; wer außer Stände ist, sein Auskommen zu
finden, dem kann noch hinreichende Unterstützung dargereicht werden.
Mit einem Worte, wir haben uns nicht zu beklagen über unsere jetzige
Lage." Ein paar einzelne Züge entheben wir noch eben diesem Rück
blick: In der Gemeinde Gais ist zu Ende 1827 eine Privatschule ent
standen, welcher ein im Fellenbergischen Institute unterrichteter Jüngling
vorsteht. Außer demjenigen, was in den gewöhnlichen Schulen gelehrt
wird, wird hier besonders der Gesangunterricht nach der Nägelischen
Methode betrieben, an welchem auch erwachsene Personen Antheil nehmen.
Ansehnliche Vermächtnisse erhielt die Gemeinde Speicher vom Raths
herrn Jakob Tobler, der am 7. Dez. 1827, 67 Jahre alt und kinderlos
starb. Er vermachte an das Kirchengut 2000 Gl., eine gleiche Summe
dem Armengut und eben so viel dem Waisenhause, endlich noch 500 Gl.
zum Bau eines neuen Pfarrhauses, im Ganzen also 6500 Gl. Dieser
Mann war von jeher sehr wohlthätigen Sinnes für die Gemeindsanstal
ten, besonders für die des Waisenhauses, für welches er durch Ankauf
von Boden und Waldungen und auf andere Weise bey 4000 Gl. ver
wendet hat.
Die Rechnung der Ersparnißkasse in Trogen am Schlusse des Jah
res 1827 zeigt ein Vermögen von 11370 Gl. 45 kr.; dagegen soll sie
an 305 Theilhaber, die Summe von 11137 Gl. 35 kr. Es bleibt ihr
also ein Vorschuß von 233 Gl. 10 kr.
Aus Appenzell-Innerrhoden meldet das Merzstück des „Ap
penzellischen Monatsblattes" was folgt: „Wie schon regelmäßig seit
5 Jahren, so erschienen auch diesesmal bey dem am 20. Merz abgehal
tenen großen zweyfachen Landrath mehrere Männer, welche ein Memorial
eingaben, das im Wesentlichen Folgendes besagt: „Tit. Schon seit
1823 wurden Ihnen alljährlich am heutigen Verfassungsrathe schriftliche
und mündliche Wünsche zur Berücksichtigung mitgetheilt, die Sie jedes
mal. Ihrer Aufmerksamkeit würdigten, was uns mit der Hoffnung be
lebte, einiges davon in Erfüllung gehen zu sehen. Unser besonderes
Augenmerk richteten wir allemal auf eine Revision der Landesgesetze.
Daß auch Sie, Tit., von der Nothwendigkeit dieser Sache überzeugt
seyen, davon gaben Sie den deutlichsten Beweis durch die Ernennung
einer Kommission, die den Auftrag erhielt, sich wöchentlich einmal zu
diesem Zweck zu versammeln, was auch wirklich einmal geschah. Das
Geschäft aber blieb dann wieder stehen und führte, unsers Wissens, zu
keinem, weitern Resultate. Tit. Wir glauben Ihnen die Wichtigkeit dee
ses Gegenstandes nicht genug schildern zu können. Das Bedürfniß einer
Revision wird von Obrigkeit und Volk täglich mehr gefühlt, und obschon
wir und mit uns ein beträchtlicher Theil unserer Mitlandsleute noch den
einten und andern Punkt zur gefälligen Erörterung einzugeben gewünscht
hätten, so unterlassen wir dieses um so eher, damit wenigstens unserm
Ansuchen wegen gedachter Revision entsprochen werde. Tit. Dieses ist
der einzigs hochwohllobl. große Rath, an dem uns unsere Verfassung ge
stattet, Wünsche und Aeußerungen demselben darzulegen. Gestützt auf
dieses Recht und beruhiget durch die Versicherung, daß Ihnen, Tit.,
das Wohl des Vaterlandes am Herzen liege, ersuchen wir Sie, uns
heute Ihre gefälligen Ansichten und bestimmte Erklärung mittheilen zu
wollen, um hievon, zum Besten des gesammten Vaterlandes, auch unsere
Mitlandsleute wieder in Kenntniß setzen zu können." Nach vielen De
batten und etwas tumultuarischen Auftritten im Rathe selbst, gieng der
Schluß über diesen Gegenstand dahin: „Die Sache soll vor die nächste
Landsgemeinde gebracht werden, und dieselbe dann eine Kommission er
nennen sowohl von Mitgliedern in als außer dem Rath, um sich mit
dem Entwurfe eines passenden Landbuches zu beschäftigen." — Zugleich

We extract a few individual details from this same review: In the municipality of Gais, a private school was established at the end of 1827, headed by a young man educated at the Fellenberg Institute. The municipality of Speicher received considerable bequests from Councillor Jakob Tobler, who died on December 7, 1827, at the age of 67 and childless. This man had always been very charitably disposed toward municipal institutions, especially the orphanage, for which he had spent nearly 4,000 guilders through the purchase of land and woodlands and in other ways.

The savings bank account in Trogen at the close of the year 1827 shows assets of 11,370 guilders, 45 kreuzers; on the other hand, it owes 305 shareholders the sum of 11,137 guilders, 35 kreuzers. It thus retains an advance of 233 guilders, 10 kreuzers.

The need for a revision is felt more daily by both the authorities and the people, and although we, along with a considerable portion of our fellow countrymen, would have wished to submit one or another point for gracious discussion, we refrain from doing so all the more readily so that at least our request for said revision may be granted. Honorable Sirs, this is the only highly honorable grand council at which our constitution permits us to present wishes and statements. Ausland.
Italien. Mailand. Der gestern erwähnte Tagsbefehl
Radetzky's lautet: „Soldaten! Ihr habt mich oft Euern Vater
genannt; als solcher wende ich mich heute an Euch. Blutige
Auftritte haben in Wien stattgefunden, unglücklicherweise veranlaßt
durch die Zwietracht, welche gegenwärtig unser theures, gemein
sames Vaterland in Parteien theilt. Der Kriegsminister, Artille
riegeneral Graf Latour, unser alter, tapferer Gefährte, ist von
einer rasenden Horde ermordet worden; der Kaiser aber und
seine Familie erfreuen sich guter Gesundheit und sind von treuen
Truppen umgeben. Soldaten! laßt Euch nicht durch falsche
Gerüchte und Lügen beirren, beharrt fest bei dem Vertrauen,
wovon Ihr mir fortwährend Beweise gegeben; ich werde Euch
die Wahrheit nicht verhehlen; seid unerschütterlich in Eurer Treue
gegen den Kaiser und in der Liebe zum Vaterland, dessen Wohl
fahrt uns Allen gleich viel am Herzen liegt. Weist mit Schmach
und Schande Jeden von Euch weg, der es wagte, Eure Treue
in Versuchung zu führen, der verlangte, daß Ihr, Sieger in so
vielen Schlachten, Eure Ehre beflecken solltet; Eure Thaten haben
die Welt mit Bewunderung erfüllt. Könige und Völker haben
es mir schriftlich bezeugt; ich trat ein als Bürge dafür, daß Ihr
in Eurer Treue und Tapferkeit beharren würdet und Ihr werdet
mein Wort nicht Lüge strafen wollen. Tapfere Waffengefährte
meiner alten Tage! Wir leben in einer Zeit trauriger Ereignisse,
gerade aber aus diesen schwierigen Kämpfen wird der Thron des
Kaisers glänzender, das Vaterland glücklicher und stärker hervor
gehen. Vergesset nicht, daß wir alle Söhne eines durch Bande,
die Jahrhunderte geheiligt haben, vereinigten Vaterlandes sind;
die verwegene Hand einiger Rebellen soll dieses herrliche Band
nicht lösen. Mein Vertrauen auf Euch ist stark und unerschüt
terlich. An Eurer Spitze sehe ich ruhig der Zukunft entgegen,
denn wir haben noch nicht vergessen, weder wie man kämpft,
noch wie man siegt. Es lebe der Kaiser! Es lebe das Vater
land!" Generalquartier Mailand, 12. Okt. Radetzky.
Deutschland. Frankfurt. Am 14. Oktober haben die
HH. Reichskommissare Teichert und Möring die Fregatte „Deutsch
land", das Kanonenboot „Sanct Pauli", die Dampfer „Ham
burg", „Lübeck" und „Bremen" sammt den darauf befindlichen
Mannschaften ganz, die Korvette „Franklin" aber unter Vorbe
halt der Genehmigung des Reichsministeriums, für die dentsche
Zentralgewalt unter entsprechender Feierlichkeit übernommen.
E. . 1 ).
— Der Belagerungszustand in Frankfurt soll an dem Tage
aufgehoben werden, an welchem das Gesetz über Schutz der Na
tionalversammlung im ganzen Umkreis der Stadt in Wirksamkeit
getreten sein wird.
Preußen. Berlin. Die auf den 18. d., den Geburts
tag des Königs angesagte Volksversammlung war nicht sehr
zahlreich besucht. — Der König empfing an diesem Tag zahl
reiche Deputationen der Volksvertreter, des Magistrats, der
Stadtverordneten, der Geistlichkeit und der Bürgerwehr. Auf
seinem Gang nach dem Dome wurde er vom Volke mit lautem
Zurufe begrüßt.
Oesterreich. Wien, 14. Okt. (Korr.) Seit dem 6. d.
ist noch kein Gewölbe geöffnet worden. Gegen 150,000 Mann
Nationalgarden, akademische Legion und Arbeiter stehen unter
den Waffen. Man hat aus ihnen eine Mobilgarde gebildet mit
20 kr. Besoldung für den Mann. Vom Gemeinderath ist eine
Bekanntmachung erschienen, daß die Wittwe eines jeden, der im
Kampfe für die gute Sache fällt, eine Pension von jährlichen
200 fl. C. M. und einen Erziehungsbeitrag von 50 fl. für jedes
Kind erhalten werde. Ebenso wird für Vermundete und Ver
krüppelte gesorgt werden. Die Wiener Garnison unter Auersperg
hat sich mit Jellachich, der mit seinem Heer und seiner Horde
vor den Linien lagert, vereinigt. Allem Anscheine nach wollen
sie die Stadt cerniren, aber nicht beschießen. Trotz der Bewaff
nung des Proletariats herrscht eine Ordnung und Sicherheit, die
beispiellos ist. Wahrlich ein herrliches Volk und werth frei zu
sein! Und doch sind wir schon seit 8 Tagen in diesem ungewissen
Zustand; noch sieht man kein Ziel, kein Ende; noch hat niemand
eine Ahnung, auch nur von der Form des Endes! — Von
Brünn kamen uns in der Nacht vom 10. auf den 11. National
garden zu Hülfe, von Grätz Studenten. Die Czechen dagegen
schmieden allerlei Ränke gegen Wien. Windischgrätz, der mit
12,000 Mann von Prag abzog, um sich der Wiener Garnison
anzuschließen, bekam vor seiner Abreise von Prag einen Fackelzug.
— Laut der A. A. Ztg. haben die Gesandten Rußland's
und England's Wien verlassen.

fahrt uns Allen gleich viel am Herzen liegt. Weist mit Schmach
und Schande Jeden von Euch weg, der es wagte, Eure Treue
in Versuchung zu führen, der verlangte, daß Ihr, Sieger in so
vielen Schlachten, Eure Ehre beflecken solltet; Eure Thaten haben
die Welt mit Bewunderung erfüllt. Könige und Völker haben
es mir schriftlich bezeugt; ich trat ein als Bürge dafür, daß Ihr
in Eurer Treue und Tapferkeit beharren würdet und Ihr werdet
mein Wort nicht Lüge strafen wollen. Tapfere Waffengefährte
meiner alten Tage! Wir leben in einer Zeit trauriger Ereignisse,
gerade aber aus diesen schwierigen Kämpfen wird der Thron des
Kaisers glänzender, das Vaterland glücklicher und stärker hervor
gehen. Vergesset nicht, daß wir alle Söhne eines durch Bande,
die Jahrhunderte geheiligt haben, vereinigten Vaterlandes sind;
die verwegene Hand einiger Rebellen soll dieses herrliche Band
nicht lösen. Mein Vertrauen auf Euch ist stark und unerschüt
terlich. An Eurer Spitze sehe ich ruhig der Zukunft entgegen,
denn wir haben noch nicht vergessen, weder wie man kämpft,
noch wie man siegt. Es lebe der Kaiser! Es lebe das Vater
land!" Generalquartier Mailand, 12. Okt. Radetzky.
Deutschland. Frankfurt. Am 14. Oktober haben die
HH. Reichskommissare Teichert und Möring die Fregatte „Deutsch
land", das Kanonenboot „Sanct Pauli", die Dampfer „Ham
burg", „Lübeck" und „Bremen" sammt den darauf befindlichen
Mannschaften ganz, die Korvette „Franklin" aber unter Vorbe
halt der Genehmigung des Reichsministeriums, für die dentsche
Zentralgewalt unter entsprechender Feierlichkeit übernommen.
E. . 1 ).
— Der Belagerungszustand in Frankfurt soll an dem Tage
aufgehoben werden, an welchem das Gesetz über Schutz der Na
tionalversammlung im ganzen Umkreis der Stadt in Wirksamkeit
getreten sein wird.
Preußen. Berlin. Die auf den 18. d., den Geburts
tag des Königs angesagte Volksversammlung war nicht sehr
zahlreich besucht. — Der König empfing an diesem Tag zahl
reiche Deputationen der Volksvertreter, des Magistrats, der
Stadtverordneten, der Geistlichkeit und der Bürgerwehr. Auf
seinem Gang nach dem Dome wurde er vom Volke mit lautem
Zurufe begrüßt.

ist noch kein Gewölbe geöffnet worden. Gegen 150,000 Mann
Nationalgarden, akademische Legion und Arbeiter stehen unter
den Waffen. Man hat aus ihnen eine Mobilgarde gebildet mit
20 kr. Besoldung für den Mann. Vom Gemeinderath ist eine
Bekanntmachung erschienen, daß die Wittwe eines jeden, der im
Kampfe für die gute Sache fällt, eine Pension von jährlichen
200 fl. C. M. und einen Erziehungsbeitrag von 50 fl. für jedes
Kind erhalten werde. Ebenso wird für Vermundete und Ver
krüppelte gesorgt werden. Die Wiener Garnison unter Auersperg
hat sich mit Jellachich, der mit seinem Heer und seiner Horde
vor den Linien lagert, vereinigt. Allem Anscheine nach wollen
sie die Stadt cerniren, aber nicht beschießen. Trotz der Bewaff
nung des Proletariats herrscht eine Ordnung und Sicherheit, die
beispiellos ist. Wahrlich ein herrliches Volk und werth frei zu
sein! Und doch sind wir schon seit 8 Tagen in diesem ungewissen
Zustand; noch sieht man kein Ziel, kein Ende; noch hat niemand
eine Ahnung, auch nur von der Form des Endes! — Von
Brünn kamen uns in der Nacht vom 10. auf den 11. National
garden zu Hülfe, von Grätz Studenten. Die Czechen dagegen
schmieden allerlei Ränke gegen Wien. Windischgrätz, der mit

anzuschließen, bekam vor seiner Abreise von Prag einen Fackelzug.

Soldiers! Do not be misled by false rumors and lies, remain steadfast in the trust you have continually shown me; I will not conceal the truth from you; be unwavering in your loyalty to the Emperor and in your love for the fatherland, whose welfare is equally dear to all of us. Shamefully reject anyone among you who dared to tempt your loyalty, who demanded that you, victors in so many battles, should stain your honor; your deeds have filled the world with admiration. Kings and peoples have attested this to me in writing; I stepped forward as a guarantor that you would persist in your loyalty and bravery, and you will not want to prove my word false. Brave comrades of my old age! We live in a time of sad events, but precisely from these difficult struggles, the Emperor's throne will emerge more glorious, the fatherland happier and stronger. Do not forget that we are all sons of a fatherland united by bonds sanctified over centuries; the reckless hand of some rebels shall not loosen this splendid bond. My trust in you is strong and unwavering. At your head, I calmly face the future, because we have not yet forgotten how to fight nor how to win. Long live the Emperor! Long live the fatherland!" General headquarters Milan, October 12. Radetzky.
Germany. Frankfurt. On October 14, the Imperial Commissioners Teichert and Möring formally took over the frigate "Deutschland," the gunboat "Sanct Pauli," the steamers "Hamburg," "Lübeck," and "Bremen" along with their crews entirely, and the corvette "Franklin" subject to approval by the Imperial Ministry, for the German central authority with appropriate ceremony.

Austria. Vienna, October 14 (Correspondence). Since the 6th, no vault has been opened. Approximately 150,000 men of the National Guard, Academic Legion, and workers are under arms. From them, a mobile guard has been formed with a pay of 20 kreuzer per man. The city council has issued an announcement that the widow of anyone who falls in battle for the good cause will receive an annual pension of 200 florins in convention currency and an education allowance of 50 florins for each child. Similarly, care will be provided for wounded and crippled individuals. The Vienna garrison under Auersperg has united with Jellachich, who is camped with his army and his horde before the lines. According to all appearances, they want to besiege the city but not bombard it. Despite the arming of the proletariat, an order and security prevail that is unprecedented. Truly a splendid people and worthy of being free! And yet we have been in this uncertain state for eight days; still, no goal, no end is seen; still, no one has any idea, even of the form of the end! — From Brünn, National Guards came to our aid during the night of the 10th to the 11th; from Graz, students. The Czechs, however, are scheming various plots against Vienna. Windischgrätz, who departed from Prague with 12,000 men to join the Vienna garrison, received a torchlight procession before his departure from Prague.
— According to the Allgemeine Zeitung, the ambassadors of Russia and England have left Vienna.

original_text:
Feuilleton 1878.
Die Pariser Welt-Ausstellung und die Volks
Schule.
Ein Gang durch die verschiedenen Länder.
K. Es ist eine neuere, glückliche Idee, mit den Welt
ausstellungen auch Schulausstellungen zu verbinden. Sie
wurde unseres Wissens zum ersten Mal in Paris 1867
versucht, kam dann in Wien 1873 und in Philadelphia
1876 zur Ausführung und jetzt wiederum und zwar in
großem Maßstab in Paris. Gegenüber andern Kultur
zweigen treten zwar die Schulen immer noch zurück, nicht
in ihren Leistungen, wohl aber in der Schätzung, die sie
erfahren. Ihnen kommt oft nicht der glücklichste Raum
zu, eine einheitliche Durchführung eines Gesammtprogramms
läßt sich kaum erkennen und das Publikum widmet ihnen
mehr nur vorübergehende Aufmerksamkeit. Und doch läßt
sich gerade hier der friedliche Wettstreit der Nationen, das
Familienleben des Volkes, am ausgeprägtesten verfolgen;
wohl auf wenig andern Gebieten werden so mannigfache
Anregungen gegeben und dieselben dann so vielfach ver
werthet wie auf dem der Schule. Erinnern wir uns z. B.
der Wiener Weltausstellung. Dort trat in den vielen
schönen Schulhäusern hauptsächlich die Schulhygiene, in
den prachtvollen Zeichenausstellungen das Bemühen, den
Volksunterricht überhaupt, wie namentlich die kunstgewerb
liche Richtung zu heben, glänzend zu Tage; hier in Paris
sind und scheinen die damals gegebenen Ideen schon Eigen
thum aller Nationen zu sein.
Kein Land hat so viel ausgestellt wie Frankreich,
keines so überraschende und unerwartete Fortschritte auf
zuweisen, wie die junge Republik. Wir, die wir gewöhn
lich der Ansicht leben, das Schulwesen Frankreichs stehe
auf einer bedenklich tiefen Stufe der Entwicklung, sind er
staunt, in vielen großen Sälen die Ausstellungen von den
verschiedensten Lehranstalten, von der Volksschule an bis
zur Hochschule hinauf, vertreten zu sehen. Die größten
Leistungen liegen hier, wie übrigens bei fast allen Staaten,
auf dem Gebiete der Geographie und des Zeichnens. Man
sieht, Niederlagen auf dem Schlachtfeld haben ihre wohl
thätigen Folgen. Wer hätte jemals diese Karten und
feinen Reliefs erwartet, wie sie z. B. das Kriegsministe
rium ausstellt, wie sie aber auch von Volksschulen ange
fertigt vorliegen. Im Zeichnen wird durchweg Schönes
geleistet; es reiht sich hier in nicht enden wollender Fülle
Stufe an Stufe; vor Allem treten die Arbeiten der ver
schiedenen Fach- und Kunstschulen hervor. Unwillkürlich
frägt man sich: Liegt nicht in diesen Spezialschulen einer
der wichtigsten Hebel der französischen Industrie und die
Erklärung des Uebergewichtes derselben über die anderen
Länder? Sieht man, wie selbst einzelne Privatgeschäfte,
für sich und aus sich allein, Fachschulen einführen und
unterhalten, so muß man die Frage bejahen und bedauern,
daß in unserm Land, der Schweiz, diesem wichtigen Unter
richtszweig nicht noch viel mehr Aufmerksamkeit geschenkt
wird, als es bisanhin geschehen. Denn wenn die Volks
schule den Zeichenunterricht erst mit dem 9. Jahre an
Hand nimmt und ihm in der Woche nur zwei Schulstun
den widmet, wenn junge Leute die bestehenden Anstalten
selten sich zu Nutze ziehen, wie es etwa bei uns geschieht,
so wird es leider noch lange gehen, bis Geschmack und feiner
Kunstsinn in unserer Industrie und unserm Handwerk
einzieht.
Italien zeigt in seiner Ausstellung deutlich, daß es
den guten Willen hat, für die Schulen etwas zu thun,
daß es aber bis anhin nicht weiter gekommen ist, als
einige gute Vorbilder zu schaffen. Die ausgestellten Schul
apparate und Instrumente sind außerordentlich schön, sie
zeugen von der Hochachtung der Behörden für die Schule
— aber wo sind solche Veranschaulichungsmittel wirklich
im Gebrauch; wo die Volksschulen, welche sie besitzen? —
Mailand stellt Arbeiten der Fröbelschulen aus, die aber
die Grenze des Zulässigen betreffend Ausführbarkeit durch
die Kinder weit überschreiten: soll das Kinderarbeit sein;
soll das zarteste Jugendalter mit solch difficilen und feinen
Aufgaben beglückt werden? Wahrlich, Fröbel, Deine An
hänger sind größer als Du, so groß, daß selbst Du ihnen
nicht mehr folgen könntest und ihnen mit Macht zurufen
würdest: Bleibt bei der Natur, lernet erst die Jugend
kennen!
Spanien macht keinen Versuch, eine Ausstellung zu
arrangiren, dagegen hat Portugal Schülerarbeiten und
das Modell einer Volksschule nach Paris gesandt. In
Wien war das portugiesische Schulhaus ein großes Ge
bäude, hier ein kleines Modell, welche beide wahrscheinlich
das Ideal der Portugiesen versinnbildlichen sollten; aber
beiderorts in ihren primitiven Verhältnissen den Vergleich
mit anderen Leistungen nicht aushalten.
Rußland stellt großentheils durch das Kriegsministe
rium aus und zwar meistens Arbeiten für und aus Mili
tärschulen; gewiß bezeichnend! Keine Ausstellungskom
mission gefällt sich so in eihnographischen Darstellungen,
wie die russische; es rücken hier eine ganze Reihe von
Puppen auf, welche die verschiedenen Völkerschaften des
großen Czarenreiches vergegenwärtigen; großer Bildungs
drang und Liebe zum Volksschulwesen ist jedoch in keinem
Gesicht derselben erkennbar. Einer bedeutungsvollen Insti
tution aber muß dennoch Erwähnung geschehen, nämlich
des pädagogischen Museums in St. Petersburg. Dasselbe
wurde im Jahr 1864 ins Leben gerusen und verbindet
mit permanenter Veranschaulichung der Lehr- und Lern
mittel aller Länder hauptsächlich den Zweck, für Gesund
heitspflege durch Vorträge, Vorweisungen und Versuche
aller Art zu wirken und in dieser Weise Zentralstelle des
ganzen Landes zu sein. Dann hat es auch die Fabrikation
von Lehrmitteln für das große, weite Reich an Hand ge
nommen und liefert z. B. physikalische Apparate, welche
denen anderer Länder kaum nachstehen dürften. Im Jahr
1866 beanspruchte das Museum einen Raum von 80 Qua
dratmetern, heute schon von 2500.
Deutschland fehlt vollständig. Man empfindet
dies als einen recht fühlbaren Mangel; hat doch in Wien
Deutschland mit seinen Schulausstellungen unbedingt Großes
geleistet und nach allen Beziehungen werthvolle Anregungen
gegeben. Begreiflicher Weise fehlt auch die Türkei.
Oesterreich erscheint getrennt als Deutschösterreich
und als Ungarn, das getreue Bild der feindlichen, sich aber
umarmenden Brüder. Oesterreich erreicht in der Ausstel
lung der Kunstgewerbeschule Wien seinen Glanzpunkt.
Wie glücklich darf sich dieses Land schätzen, ein solches In
stitut zu besitzen. Mit beredten, gewaltigen Worten legt
dasselbe Zeugniß ab, wie die Industrie eines Volkes durch
allgemeine und durch Fachschulen gehoben werden kann
und wie von einer gut geleiteten Zentralschule aus Ge
schmack und Richtung im Kunsthandwerk vortheilhaft be
stimmt wird. Wo gibt es aber auch mehr Kunstgewerbe
schulen als in Oesterreich, wo ist der Zusammenhang der
selben und die Verbindung mit der Zentralstelle inniger
als gerade hier? — Ungarn sucht in letzter Zeit auf
dem Gebiete der Volksbildung Vieles nachzuholen, das be
weisen seine großartigen Schulhausbaupläne, seine Samm
lungen seiner physikalischer Apparate. (Schluß folgt.)

kennen!

Feuilleton 1878.
The Paris World Exhibition and the Public School.
A Tour Through Various Countries.

It is a recent, fortunate idea to combine world exhibitions with school exhibitions. To our knowledge, this was first attempted in Paris in 1867, then implemented in Vienna in 1873 and in Philadelphia in 1876, and now once again, and on a large scale, in Paris. Compared to other branches of culture, schools still take a back seat—not in their achievements, but certainly in the appreciation they receive. They are often not allotted the most favorable space; a unified execution of an overall program is hardly discernible, and the public devotes to them only passing attention. And yet, it is precisely here that the peaceful competition of nations, the family life of the people, can be most distinctly observed; indeed, in few other areas are such diverse inspirations provided and then so extensively utilized as in that of the school. Let us recall, for example, the Vienna World Exhibition. There, in the many beautiful school buildings, school hygiene shone brilliantly, and in the magnificent drawing exhibitions, the effort to elevate public education in general, and particularly the direction of arts and crafts, was splendidly evident; here in Paris, the ideas given then already seem to be the property of all nations.

No country has exhibited as much as France, none shows such surprising and unexpected progress as the young Republic. We, who usually hold the opinion that the school system of France stands at a worryingly low level of development, are astonished to see in many large halls exhibitions from the most diverse educational institutions, from the public school up to the university. The greatest achievements here, as indeed with almost all states, lie in the fields of geography and drawing. One sees that defeats on the battlefield have their beneficial consequences. Who would ever have expected such maps and fine reliefs as are exhibited, for example, by the Ministry of War, but which are also produced by public schools. In drawing, beautiful work is consistently achieved; here, in an endless abundance, one level follows another; above all, the works of the various trade and art schools stand out. One involuntarily asks oneself: Does not one of the most important levers of French industry, and the explanation of its predominance over other countries, lie in these specialized schools? When one sees how even individual private businesses, on their own and by themselves, introduce and maintain trade schools, one must answer the question in the affirmative and regret that in our country, Switzerland, this important branch of instruction is not given much more attention than has been the case until now. For if the public school only takes up drawing instruction at the age of 9 and devotes only two school hours per week to it, if young people rarely take advantage of the existing institutions, as is the case with us, then unfortunately it will be a long time before taste and refined artistic sense enter our industry and our crafts.

Italy clearly shows in its exhibition that it has the good will to do something for the schools, but that until now it has not progressed further than creating some good models. The exhibited school apparatuses and instruments are extraordinarily beautiful; they testify to the authorities' high regard for the school—but where are such illustrative aids actually in use; where are the public schools that possess them? — Milan exhibits works from Froebel schools, but these far exceed the limit of what is permissible regarding feasibility by children: is this supposed to be children's work; is the most tender youth to be blessed with such difficult and delicate tasks? Truly, Froebel, your followers are greater than you, so great that even you could no longer follow them and would call out to them with force: Stay with nature, first get to know youth!

Spain makes no attempt to arrange an exhibition; on the other hand, Portugal has sent student works and a model of a public school to Paris. In Vienna, the Portuguese schoolhouse was a large building; here, a small model, both of which probably were meant to symbolize the ideal of the Portuguese; but in both places, in their primitive conditions, they cannot withstand comparison with other achievements.

Russia exhibits largely through the Ministry of War, mostly works for and from military schools; certainly telling! No exhibition commission delights so much in ethnographic representations as the Russian; here a whole series of dolls marches forth, representing the various peoples of the great Tsarist empire; however, no great thirst for education and love for the public school system is discernible in any of their faces. Yet mention must be made of one significant institution, namely the Pedagogical Museum in St. Petersburg. It was established in the year 1864 and combines, with a permanent display of teaching and learning aids from all countries, mainly the purpose of promoting health care through lectures, demonstrations, and experiments of all kinds, and in this way to be the central institution of the entire country. Then it has also taken up the manufacture of teaching aids for the large, vast empire and supplies, for example, physical apparatuses that are scarcely inferior to those of other countries. In the year 1866, the museum claimed a space of 80 square meters; today already 2500.

Germany is completely absent. One feels this as a very palpable lack; for in Vienna, Germany, with its school exhibitions, undoubtedly achieved great things and provided valuable inspirations in all respects. Understandably, Turkey is also missing.

Austria appears separately as German Austria and as Hungary, the faithful image of hostile but embracing brothers. Austria reaches its zenith in the exhibition of the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts. How fortunate this country may consider itself to possess such an institute. With eloquent, powerful words, it bears witness to how the industry of a people can be elevated through general and through specialized schools, and how, from a well-led central school, taste and direction in arts and crafts are advantageously determined. But where are there more arts and crafts schools than in Austria, where is their connection and the link with the central institution more intimate than precisely here? — Hungary has recently sought to make up for much in the field of public education, as evidenced by its grand school building plans, its collections of physical apparatuses. (To be continued.)

Die geplante Verwüstung des Alten Rheins
Zum Entsetzen aller, die davon hören, soll eine der
schönsten Flußlandschaften der Ostschweiz (und der
Schweiz überhaupt) dem Moloch der Zivilisation zum
Opfer gebracht und mit einem (vorläufigen!) Kosten
aufwand von rund 1,6 Millionen Franken von
Grund aus und für alle Zeiten vernichtet werden.
Wäre der massive Plan eine rein st.-gallische Kan
tonsangelegenheit, so bliebe uns andern nichts übrig,
als tatenlos zur Seite zu treten und trauernden
Herzens zuzusehen, daß man in einem Winkel unseres
Vaterlandes wieder einmal nicht begreifen will, wie
sehr auch die aus sich selbst gewordene Natur eines
wird, dazu schweigend seine Duldung zu geben und sich
nicht aufzulehnen gegen ein Vorhaben, das einzig
artige Landschaftsreize unrettbar vernichtet.
Und der Kenner des alten Rheintals und besonders
seines unvergleichlichen Mündungsdeltas gibt's viele!
Denn zu Tausenden kommen während der guten
Jahreszeiten die Menschen zu Fuß und im Auto, mit
der Bahn, dem Ruder-, Motor- oder Segelschiff aus
nah und fern, um wenigstens für ein paar Stunden,
wenn es geht, auch für etliche Wochen, ihren Augen
eine Wohltat zu erweisen und sich rheinauf oder
rheinab am Fluß entlang zu ergehen, der sanft und
bestimmten Landschaftsraumes zu jenen idealen
Werten gehört, die es zu achten und zu bewahren gilt
und die man mit allen zur Verfügung stehenden
Mitteln zu verteidigen habe, wenn Interessen, die sich
zufälligerweise berechnen lassen, daran gehen, das zu
untergraben, was sich durch ein gemeinsames Maß
nicht ausdrücken läßt. Da jedoch der Bund 80 Prozent
an die Kosten wird zahlen müssen, geht das Vorhaben
nicht nur die St. Galler an, sondern alle, die wissen,
daß wir schon längst nicht mehr so dick im Reichtum
sitzen, daß man die immer seltener werdenden land
schaftlichen Kleinodien unserer Voralpenlandschaft
einfach verschleudern darf.
Es handelt sich bei dem in Frage stehenden Pro
jekt um die Umgestaltung des als „Alter Rhein"
bezeichneten, reichgewundenen Wasserarms, der als
Jahrzeichen der zwischen St. Margrethen und Boden
see liegenden Niederungen das ganze sogenannte Alte
Kheintal beherrscht (siehe Situationsbild). Bevor der
bei Fußach mündende Rheinkanal angelegt und damit
ein direkter Abfluß des Stroms in das große See
becken geschaffen wurde, ergossen sich die Wasser des
Oberrheins durch diesen Arm in den Bodensee, und
oft war sein Bett viel zu eng, um sie zu fassen. Ob
gleich er seit dem Fußacher Durchstich nur noch die
überschüssigen Stauwasser des Kanals und die Wasser
der anschließenden Bäche dem Bodensee zuführen darf.
ist er immer noch ein stattlicher Fluß, der zwischen

The Planned Devastation of the Old Rhine

To the horror of all who hear of it, one of the most beautiful river landscapes in Eastern Switzerland (and in Switzerland overall) is to be sacrificed to the Moloch of civilization and, with a (tentative!) cost expenditure of around 1.6 million francs, utterly and forever destroyed.

If this massive plan were purely a matter for the canton of St. Gallen, we others would have nothing left but to step aside helplessly and, with grieving hearts, watch as once again in a corner of our homeland they refuse to understand how much nature, having become what it is by its own forces, is a thing of value, silently giving their consent and not rebelling against a project that irrevocably destroys unique scenic charms.

And there are many who know the old Rhine valley and especially its incomparable mouth delta! For thousands come during the good seasons, by foot and by car, by train, by rowing, motor, or sailing boat from near and far, to grant their eyes a treat for at least a few hours, if possible even for several weeks, and to wander along the river upstream or downstream, which gently and majestically flows through its predetermined landscape space, belonging to those ideal values that must be respected and preserved and defended with all available means, when interests that happen to be calculable proceed to undermine what cannot be expressed by a common measure. However, since the federal government will have to pay 80 percent of the costs, the project concerns not only the people of St. Gallen, but all who know that we are no longer so flush with wealth that we can simply squander the increasingly rare scenic gems of our pre-Alpine landscape.

The project in question involves the transformation of the richly winding water branch designated as the "Old Rhine," which as the year-mark of the lowlands lying between St. Margrethen and Lake Constance dominates the entire so-called Old Rhine valley (see situation picture). Before the Rhine canal discharging at Fußach was constructed and thereby a direct outflow of the river into the large lake basin was created, the waters of the Upper Rhine poured through this branch into Lake Constance, and often its bed was much too narrow to contain them. Although since the Fußach cut it may only carry the excess dammed waters of the canal and the waters of the adjoining streams to Lake Constance, it is still a substantial river that strives toward its goal between natural banks and expands to an average width of 160 to 200 meters.

The incomprehensible plan now aims to turn this water branch, which shapes the face of the entire region and which the Rhine dug for itself countless centuries ago, into a water channel with bound banks, which between St. Margrethen and Rheineck has a bed width of only 16.5 meters and between Rheineck and the mouth has a width of 20 meters, thus roughly only a tenth of the old expanse. In the mouth area, moreover, strong wave breakers and inner guide dams are to be built, which must correspondingly tower high above the water level to be effective at all. But the most absurd and improbable thing is that the authors of this plan want to make us believe that the existing landscape image, for whose form the eternal forces of nature are essentially responsible, will be hardly affected by all these measures and that the project is completely in harmony with the admonition also issued from the federal house to the canton of St. Gallen, that "in the execution of the project, the preservation of the landscape image must be taken into account as far as possible." For only then does the Confederation open its purse.

The plan is to create a water channel with bound banks, which between St. Margrethen and Rheineck has a bed width of only 16.5 meters and between Rheineck and the mouth a width of 20 meters, thus roughly only a tenth of the old expanse. In the mouth area, moreover, strong wave breakers and inner guide dams are to be built, which must correspondingly tower high above the water level to be effective at all. But the most absurd and improbable thing is that the authors of this plan want to make us believe that the existing landscape image, for whose form the eternal forces of nature are essentially responsible, will be hardly affected by all these measures and that the project is completely in harmony with the admonition also issued from the federal house to the canton of St. Gallen, that "in the execution of the project, the preservation of the landscape image must be taken into account as far as possible." For only then does the Confederation open its purse.

The painters come, the poets come, the schools come, to whom one wishes to present an unpretentious, lovely, and yet unforgettable piece of their homeland, and they all learn to love the landscape that welcomes them. Magnificent banks, which may silt up as they please, line the now tranquil old river course, and behind the wall of the bright riparian forest strips, whose wonderful willows, poplars, birches, and pines are here as much in their element as the herons and the diverse waterfowl and shorebird folk, the old dikes, flanked by strangely gnarled trees, stretch crisscross through the flat land, whose agriculturally used areas open toward the Rhine point onto immense reed meadows, reed forests, a splendid beach, and water holes with water lilies... For all of them, the intact preservation of the Old Rhine is a fervent, very fervent wish.

But those to whom the word Old Rhine means nothing will, by looking at the accompanying pictures upward and downward, sufficiently guess what will perish here when the river is narrowed to a water thread of 20 meters bed width by gravel groynes, which are to be constructed along and across its course at regular intervals, and dead sludge bays are created right and left of the central channel, which they hope will silt up slowly by themselves over time.

Of course, the originators, operators, and beneficiaries of the construction plan also have their reasons for justifying the enterprise. They are consistently of a local-economic nature and need not be discussed here any more than the costs of the new plan, which are "still very high," but are nevertheless ready to comply.

Because the policy of money distribution slowly grown out of the crisis situation of our country has made it possible to classify the entire project among the job creation measures of the Confederation. This circumstance has — it cannot be denied — undeservedly and unrelated to the true value of the enterprise — helped the initiators of the transformation idea to a very strong position among the Rhine valley population and some parties, and it apparently also overthrown the last reservations at the central government.

For all these reasons, it is today almost hopeless to still run against the project. The National Council and the Council of States believed they had to agree because the execution creates work and everyone sincerely wishes everyone the ability to earn or re-earn. The St. Gallen homeland protection section has therefore already decided not to oppose the project, despite its murderous tendencies, insofar as the construction of the stretch from St. Margrethen to the customs house, a point at the beginning of the actual mouth delta below Rheineck, is concerned.

However, against the alteration of the lowest section, lying by the village of Altenrhein, which extends from the customs house to the outflow of the water branch into Lake Constance (see the pictures) — and this is important — the homeland protection commission also protests, because it would consider it a forgetfulness of duty and a gross violation of its responsibility toward posterity if it also remained silent about this barbarity.

We likewise believe that everything must be done to prevent any transformative intervention in this last, most beautiful, and most characteristic stretch of the old Rhine course! Let the intervention be called whatever it may, and let it be masked as the economic, political, and technical spirit of the initiators may always please: — it must in every case be abstained from! The entire area from the customs house downward to the mouth strip lying in the backwater area of Lake Constance must therefore be declared inviolable by the federal government, and this inviolability must be imposed on the canton of St. Gallen as a servitude or unlimited easement toward the Swiss people.

What is suggested here is the minimum of consideration that can still be demanded now. Unfortunately, it is indeed also already the last!

For everyone who knows the area, the heart bleeds and anger rises to the temples when it is demanded of him to accept the destruction of this landscape jewel, which is not only a scenic but also a cultural asset of the highest order. And this is independent of the question, not uncontested by experts, whether the present project from a purely water engineering standpoint is really the best and whether in case of execution it will really fulfill all hopes and future prognoses connected with it. The material on these questions is laid down in countless documents and lastly in the message of the Federal Council of May 6 of this year, in which our highest national authority — albeit with strong reluctance — recommends to the federal assembly the approval of a fifty percent contribution to the costs estimated at 1,565,000 francs. It suffices to mention that the Federal Council has resisted for forty years the transformation project, which has assumed ever larger dimensions and ever more radical forms, and has given the canton of St. Gallen more than one refusal. The Planned Devastation of the Old Rhine

To the horror of all who hear of it, one of the most beautiful river landscapes in Eastern Switzerland (and in Switzerland overall) is to be sacrificed to the Moloch of civilization and, with a (tentative!) cost expenditure of around 1.6 million francs, utterly and forever destroyed.

If this massive plan were purely a matter for the canton of St. Gallen, we others would have nothing left but to step aside helplessly and, with grieving hearts, watch as once again in a corner of our homeland they refuse to understand how much nature, having become what it is by its own forces, is a thing of value, silently giving their consent and not rebelling against a project that irrevocably destroys unique scenic charms.

And there are many who know the old Rhine valley and especially its incomparable mouth delta! For thousands come during the good seasons, by foot and by car, by train, by rowing, motor, or sailing boat from near and far, to grant their eyes a treat for at least a few hours, if possible even for several weeks, and to wander along the river upstream or downstream, which gently and majestically flows through its predetermined landscape space, belonging to those ideal values that must be respected and preserved and defended with all available means, when interests that happen to be calculable proceed to undermine what cannot be expressed by a common measure. However, since the federal government will have to pay 80 percent of the costs, the project concerns not only the people of St. Gallen, but all who know that we are no longer so flush with wealth that we can simply squander the increasingly rare scenic gems of our pre-Alpine landscape.

The project in question involves the transformation of the richly winding water branch designated as the "Old Rhine," which as the year-mark of the lowlands lying between St. Margrethen and Lake Constance dominates the entire so-called Old Rhine valley (see situation picture). Before the Rhine canal discharging at Fußach was constructed and thereby a direct outflow of the river into the large lake basin was created, the waters of the Upper Rhine poured through this branch into Lake Constance, and often its bed was much too narrow to contain them. Although since the Fußach cut it may only carry the excess dammed waters of the canal and the waters of the adjoining streams to Lake Constance, it is still a substantial river that strives toward its goal between natural banks and expands to an average width of 160 to 200 meters.

The incomprehensible plan now aims to turn this water branch, which shapes the face of the entire region and which the Rhine dug for itself countless centuries ago, into a water channel with bound banks, which between St. Margrethen and Rheineck has a bed width of only 16.5 meters and between Rheineck and the mouth has a width of 20 meters, thus roughly only a tenth of the old expanse. In the mouth area, moreover, strong wave breakers and inner guide dams are to be built, which must correspondingly tower high above the water level to be effective at all. But the most absurd and improbable thing is that the authors of this plan want to make us believe that the existing landscape image, for whose form the eternal forces of nature are essentially responsible, will be hardly affected by all these measures and that the project is completely in harmony with the admonition also issued from the federal house to the canton of St. Gallen, that "in the execution of the project, the preservation of the landscape image must be taken into account as far as possible." For only then does the Confederation open its purse.

The plan is to create a water channel with bound banks, which between St. Margrethen and Rheineck has a bed width of only 16.5 meters and between Rheineck and the mouth a width of 20 meters, thus roughly only a tenth of the old expanse. In the mouth area, moreover, strong wave breakers and inner guide dams are to be built, which must correspondingly tower high above the water level to be effective at all. But the most absurd and improbable thing is that the authors of this plan want to make us believe that the existing landscape image, for whose form the eternal forces of nature are essentially responsible, will be hardly affected by all these measures and that the project is completely in harmony with the admonition also issued from the federal house to the canton of St. Gallen, that "in the execution of the project, the preservation of the landscape image must be taken into account as far as possible." For only then does the Confederation open its purse.

The painters come, the poets come, the schools come, to whom one wishes to present an unpretentious, lovely, and yet unforgettable piece of their homeland, and they all learn to love the landscape that welcomes them. Magnificent banks, which may silt up as they please, line the now tranquil old river course, and behind the wall of the bright riparian forest strips, whose wonderful willows, poplars, birches, and pines are here as much in their element as the herons and the diverse waterfowl and shorebird folk, the old dikes, flanked by strangely gnarled trees, stretch crisscross through the flat land, whose agriculturally used areas open toward the Rhine point onto immense reed meadows, reed forests, a splendid beach, and water holes with water lilies... For all of them, the intact preservation of the Old Rhine is a fervent, very fervent wish.

But those to whom the word Old Rhine means nothing will, by looking at the accompanying pictures upward and downward, sufficiently guess what will perish here when the river is narrowed to a water thread of 20 meters bed width by gravel groynes, which are to be constructed along and across its course at regular intervals, and dead sludge bays are created right and left of the central channel, which they hope will silt up slowly by themselves over time.

Of course, the originators, operators, and beneficiaries of the construction plan also have their reasons for justifying the enterprise. They are consistently of a local-economic nature and need not be discussed here any more than the costs of the new plan, which are "still very high," but are nevertheless ready to comply.

Because the policy of money distribution slowly grown out of the crisis situation of our country has made it possible to classify the entire project among the job creation measures of the Confederation. This circumstance has — it cannot be denied — undeservedly and unrelated to the true value of the enterprise — helped the initiators of the transformation idea to a very strong position among the Rhine valley population and some parties, and it apparently also overthrown the last reservations at the central government.

For all these reasons, it is today almost hopeless to still run against the project. The National Council and the Council of States believed they had to agree because the execution creates work and everyone sincerely wishes everyone the ability to earn or re-earn. The St. Gallen homeland protection section has therefore already decided not to oppose the project, despite its murderous tendencies, insofar as the construction of the stretch from St. Margrethen to the customs house, a point at the beginning of the actual mouth delta below Rheineck, is concerned.

However, against the alteration of the lowest section, lying by the village of Altenrhein, which extends from the customs house to the outflow of the water branch into Lake Constance (see the pictures) — and this is important — the homeland protection commission also protests, because it would consider it a forgetfulness of duty and a gross violation of its responsibility toward posterity if it also remained silent about this barbarity.

We likewise believe that everything must be done to prevent any transformative intervention in this last, most beautiful, and most characteristic stretch of the old Rhine course! Let the intervention be called whatever it may, and let it be masked as the economic, political, and technical spirit of the initiators may always please: — it must in every case be abstained from! The entire area from the customs house downward to the mouth strip lying in the backwater area of Lake Constance must therefore be declared inviolable by the federal government, and this inviolability must be imposed on the canton of St. Gallen as a servitude or unlimited easement toward the Swiss people.

What is suggested here is the minimum of consideration that can still be demanded now. Unfortunately, it is indeed also already the last!

For everyone who knows the area, the heart bleeds and anger rises to the temples when it is demanded of him to accept the destruction of this landscape jewel, which is not only a scenic but also a cultural asset of the highest order. And this is independent of the question, not uncontested by experts, whether the present project from a purely water engineering standpoint is really the best and whether in case of execution it will really fulfill all hopes and future prognoses connected with it. The material on these questions is laid down in countless documents and lastly in the message of the Federal Council of May 6 of this year, in which our highest national authority — albeit with strong reluctance — recommends to the federal assembly the approval of a fifty percent contribution to the costs estimated at 1,565,000 francs. It suffices to mention that the Federal Council has resisted for forty years the transformation project, which has assumed ever larger dimensions and ever more radical forms, and has given the canton of St. Gallen more than one refusal. For the construction of a second track of the Berlin-Charlottenburg horse-drawn railway, the definitive concession has been granted to the company, and the execution can proceed. The funds for the construction of the second track will probably be raised through the exchange of new shares; it is intended to issue one new share at par for each old share, as soon as the company deems it desirable. Regarding the time when the dividend approved at the last general meeting will be paid out, the B.B.-C. writes: "It will be recalled that the board of the Märkisch-Schlesischen Maschinen-Fabrik, formerly Egells, was to decide on the time for payment, and it was of the justified opinion that the payout should not take place until the company could proceed with it without any weakening of its cash reserves. This point in time is likely not far off now, as the company's business has taken a very gratifying upswing recently. Thus, it is reported that the boiler-making works of the company in Silesia has recently received orders amounting to 250,000 thalers; likewise, the local machine factory has received significant orders for naval purposes, which will keep it busy for a longer period. In some time, a supervisory board meeting of the Märkisch-Schlesischen Maschinenfabrik will convene, which was the intention of the general meeting's resolution, to determine the timing for the dividend payment and will decide on the payout date."

The dividend of the Siegen, Schwefelsiles joint-stock company has been set at 2 percent.

At the general meeting of the Wagon and Locomotive Works held in Hamm on the 23rd of this month, votes of discharge were granted. The retiring members of the administration were re-elected, and in the extraordinary general meeting following the ordinary general meeting, the liquidation of the company was resolved in accordance with the management's proposal. The report of the supervisory board states that a fruitful cooperation of the management appointed in February of last year proved unattainable, and that consequently in the month of April, the construction of the locomotive factory decided in March had been suspended up to that point, that a reorganization of the management took place and was specifically motivated by the factory facilities. The report further mentions the amount of 225,000 thalers, which a number of shareholders of the company had gratuitously remitted to cover the excess losses. The shares of the company are valued at 40 percent, but the situation of the company is still hopeless today. The delivery contracts found by the new management could not be fulfilled on time even with the utmost effort, as the deadlines had partly already expired by the end of the past year: this resulted in penalty clauses for almost all deliveries, of which only one case has been settled so far, while negotiations are still pending for the settlement of the last case. The balance sheet presented by the management has been examined by a commission from among the shareholders and found to be in agreement with the books. The depreciation on real estate, machinery, and utensils, which the management has undertaken, appears justified by the circumstances, especially by the devaluation of all movable and immovable property values that occurred in recent years.

At the general meeting of the Wagon and Locomotive Works, 44 shareholders were present, representing 6749 shares with 856 votes. The meeting took note of the administration's report and granted discharge to the management with 836 votes against 20.

As already mentioned earlier, this only concerns a transformation of the company from a limited partnership with shares into a pure joint-stock company. This will be constituted shortly, and the supervisory board will consist of: Privy Commercial Councillor Zwicker for the firm Gebrüder Schickler; Privy Commercial Councillor v. Bleichröder for the firm S. Bleichröder; Mr. Schüler for the firm F. Mart. Magnus; Consul v. Oppenfeld for the firm M. Oppenheim's Sons; and Privy Commission Councillor R. Wentzel, who acts as delegate of the supervisory board. The management will consist of the hitherto registered directors: Dr. Rasche, Dr. Rosenstein, and Dr. Fuchs. In the nature of the enterprise, therefore, no change will occur.

For the construction of a second track of the Berlin-Charlottenburg horse-drawn railway, the definitive concession has been granted to the company, and the execution can proceed. The funds for the construction of the second track will probably be raised through the exchange of new shares; it is intended to issue one new share at par for each old share, as soon as the company deems it desirable. However, nothing has yet been decided in this regard.

Regarding the time when the dividend approved at the last general meeting will be paid out, the B.B.-C. writes: "It will be recalled that the board of the Märkisch-Schlesischen Maschinen-Fabrik, formerly Egells, was to decide on the time for payment, and it was of the justified opinion that the payout should not take place until the company could proceed with it without any weakening of its cash reserves. This point in time is likely not far off now, as the company's business has taken a very gratifying upswing recently. Thus, it is reported that the boiler-making works of the company in Silesia has recently received orders amounting to 250,000 thalers; likewise, the local machine factory has received significant orders for naval purposes, which will keep it busy for a longer period. In some time, a supervisory board meeting of the Märkisch-Schlesischen Maschinenfabrik will convene, which was the intention of the general meeting's resolution, to determine the timing for the dividend payment and will decide on the payout date."

At the meeting of the supervisory board of the Bauerwitz sugar factory joint-stock company held on the 15th of this month, it was resolved to propose to the general meeting on September 24, for the business year ending August 1, the distribution of a dividend of 10 percent, and beyond the statutory depreciation of about 15,000 thalers, further...

The dividend of the Siegen, Schwefelsiles joint-stock company has been set at 2 percent.

The general meeting of the Westphalia machine factory shareholders has subsequently approved the distribution of a dividend. This quarterly amount beyond the expenses incurred. The aforementioned sum had previously been used for depreciation. In the re-election of the supervisory board, Banker Russ Flema A. Russ Jr., in Berlin, was elected. The factory is for three in Hagen approved the motion that the 37,000 thalers due from the Quistorp's bankruptcy estate upon receipt be distributed among...

At the general meeting of the Wagon and Locomotive Works held in Hamm on the 23rd of this month, votes of discharge were granted. The retiring members of the administration were re-elected, and in the extraordinary general meeting following the ordinary general meeting, the liquidation of the company was resolved in accordance with the management's proposal. The report of the supervisory board states that a fruitful cooperation of the management appointed in February of last year proved unattainable, and that consequently in the month of April, the construction of the locomotive factory decided in March had been suspended up to that point, that a reorganization of the management took place and was specifically motivated by the factory facilities. The report further mentions the amount of 225,000 thalers, which a number of shareholders of the company had gratuitously remitted to cover the excess losses. The shares of the company are valued at 40 percent, but the situation of the company is still hopeless today. The delivery contracts found by the new management could not be fulfilled on time even with the utmost effort, as the deadlines had partly already expired by the end of the past year: this resulted in penalty clauses for almost all deliveries, of which only one case has been settled so far, while negotiations are still pending for the settlement of the last case. The balance sheet presented by the management has been examined by a commission from among the shareholders and found to be in agreement with the books. The depreciation on real estate, machinery, and utensils, which the management has undertaken, appears justified by the circumstances, especially by the devaluation of all movable and immovable property values that occurred in recent years.

At the general meeting of the Wagon and Locomotive Works, 44 shareholders were present, representing 6749 shares with 856 votes. The meeting took note of the administration's report and granted discharge to the management with 836 votes against 20.

Italy.
Piedmont. In recent days, there has been great activity in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Count Pes di Villamarina, chargé d'affaires at the French court, as well as Marquis d'Azeglio, chargé d'affaires at the Court of St. James, have been in Turin for several days and have held frequent and lengthy conferences with Prime Minister Count Cavour.

For some time, several Piedmontese newspapers have complained about the manner in which the authorities have handled the libraries found in the abolished monasteries. These complaints are raised particularly in the interest of the sciences and historical studies, which have been deprived of irreplaceable treasures by this vandalistic system. The "Gazzetta Piemontese" now believes it must respond with a statement, explaining the government's actions as "completely lawful"—which, of course, says very little.

The "Courrier des Alpes," a newspaper published in Savoy, which we should note here seems to respect treaty-based rights as little as the "Opinione," "Unione," etc., published in Turin, in its profession of faith regarding Piedmont's policy toward Austria, has Prince Carignano making a mysterious journey to the north of Germany to conclude, if not a defensive and offensive alliance, at least a neutrality treaty with Prussia for the war "to which Piedmont is preparing against Austria." Turin, October 11. Preparations are already being made in Villafranca to ceremoniously hand over the keys of the arsenal to the captain of the frigate Polkan, who is equipped with the necessary powers to take possession of the place. However, according to the "Presse," the ceremony is to take place only after the arrival of the Russian fleet, which, according to the latest news, was anchored off Brest and is expected to arrive in Villafranca almost simultaneously with Admiral Grand Duke Constantine. The festivities in Villafranca will continue and conclude in Nice with a religious ceremony; the Prince will lay the foundation stone for a Greek church there, as such a church is deemed necessary wherever Russians reside in larger numbers. In 1856, the Empress Mother had a chapel in the Villa Avigdor; however, due to limited space, it could not accommodate all the faithful staying in Nice. Two years ago, Grand Duke Constantine came to La Spezia on the flagship Viborg to inspect the location. Now it is quite possible that Villafranca does not offer enough security for large ships and that it is planned to send those ships, which Russia maintains in the Mediterranean Sea, to La Spezia during the winter. While the Tsardom is settling in Piedmont, France is gaining an increasingly firm foothold in Civitavecchia. There, too, fortifications are being carried out on a large scale. Shortly after the French entry in 1849, the engineers strengthened the place on the land side by constructing covered galleries on the ramparts with fascines and gabions. But now far more extensive works are being undertaken. The city is being expanded in the direction of the Roman Gate (road to Rome). The railway will have its endpoint within the new ramparts and will pass under the batteries. Toward the Corneto Gate, there will be no extension of the walls; instead, two redoubts are to protect this part located near the inner harbor. (M. I.)
