Spezzia, um die Localität in Augenschein zu nehmen.
Nun ist es leicht möglich, daß Villafranca für große
Schiffe nicht Sicherheit genug darbietet, und daß man
sich vornimmt, während des Winters jene nach La
Spezzia zu senden, welche Rußland im mittelländischen
Meere unterhalten wird. Während so das Czaren»
thum in Piémont sich häuslich einrichtet, faßt Frank«
reich immer festeren Fuß in Civitavecchia. Auch da
werden Befestigungen in großem Maßstabe
ausgeführt. Bald nach dem Einrücken der Franzosen im
Jahre 1849 verstärkte das Genie den Platz nach der
Landseite zu durch Aufführung von bedeckten Gallerten
auf den Wällen mit Faschinen und Schanzkörben. Jetzt
aber werden weit umfassendere Arbeiten vorgenommen.
Tie Stadt wird in der Richtung nach dem römischen
Thor (Straße nach Nom) vergrößert. Tie Eisenbahn
wird ihren Endpunct innerhalb der neuen Umwallung
finden und unter den Batterien hindurchfühlen. Nach
dem Thor von Cornctto zu wird zwar keine
Ausdehnung der Wälle stattfinden, dafür sollen zwei Redon»
tcn diesen in der Nachbarschaft des innern Hafens
gelegenen Thcil beschützen. (M. I.)

Italy.
Piedmont. In recent days, there has been great activity in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Count Pes di Villamarina, chargé d'affaires at the French court, as well as Marquis d'Azeglio, chargé d'affaires at the Court of St. James, have been in Turin for several days and have held frequent and lengthy conferences with Prime Minister Count Cavour.

For some time, several Piedmontese newspapers have complained about the manner in which the authorities have handled the libraries found in the abolished monasteries. These complaints are raised particularly in the interest of the sciences and historical studies, which have been deprived of irreplaceable treasures by this vandalistic system. The "Gazzetta Piemontese" now believes it must respond with a statement, explaining the government's actions as "completely lawful"—which, of course, says very little.

The "Courrier des Alpes," a newspaper published in Savoy, which we should note here seems to respect treaty-based rights as little as the "Opinione," "Unione," etc., published in Turin, in its profession of faith regarding Piedmont's policy toward Austria, has Prince Carignano making a mysterious journey to the north of Germany to conclude, if not a defensive and offensive alliance, at least a neutrality treaty with Prussia for the war "to which Piedmont is preparing against Austria." Turin, October 11. Preparations are already being made in Villafranca to ceremoniously hand over the keys of the arsenal to the captain of the frigate Polkan, who is equipped with the necessary powers to take possession of the place. However, according to the "Presse," the ceremony is to take place only after the arrival of the Russian fleet, which, according to the latest news, was anchored off Brest and is expected to arrive in Villafranca almost simultaneously with Admiral Grand Duke Constantine. The festivities in Villafranca will continue and conclude in Nice with a religious ceremony; the Prince will lay the foundation stone for a Greek church there, as such a church is deemed necessary wherever Russians reside in larger numbers. In 1856, the Empress Mother had a chapel in the Villa Avigdor; however, due to limited space, it could not accommodate all the faithful staying in Nice. Two years ago, Grand Duke Constantine came to La Spezia on the flagship Viborg to inspect the location. Now it is quite possible that Villafranca does not offer enough security for large ships and that it is planned to send those ships, which Russia maintains in the Mediterranean Sea, to La Spezia during the winter. While the Tsardom is settling in Piedmont, France is gaining an increasingly firm foothold in Civitavecchia. There, too, fortifications are being carried out on a large scale. Shortly after the French entry in 1849, the engineers strengthened the place on the land side by constructing covered galleries on the ramparts with fascines and gabions. But now far more extensive works are being undertaken. The city is being expanded in the direction of the Roman Gate (road to Rome). The railway will have its endpoint within the new ramparts and will pass under the batteries. Toward the Corneto Gate, there will be no extension of the walls; instead, two redoubts are to protect this part located near the inner harbor. (M. I.)

original_text:
Nochenschau.
Die Alabamafrage, die mehr und mehr in den Vor
dergrund tritt, besteht aus zwei Forderungen. Einmal
wird von Nordamerika Entschädigung verlangt für die
nordischen Kauffahrer, welche von den in England ge
kauften und bewaffneten Korsaren wie Alabama, Georgia,
Florida, Sumter u. s. w. während dem Bürgerkrieg ge
kapert und verbrannt worden sind. Dann wird aber
England auch der Verletzung des Völkerrechts beschul
digt, indem es in seinen Häfen die Ausrüstung von
sonderbündischen Kaperschiffen zugelassen hat. Von Wa
shington aus wurde nun ein Schiedsgericht über beide
Fragen vorgeschlagen, während England sich wohl für
die erste Frage einem Schiedsgericht unterziehen wollte,
hingegen keine Intervention in seine innere Verkehrs
politik dulden will. Da nun die Vereinigten Staaten
auf eine Ausscheidung beider Punkte nicht eingehen woll
ten, so wurden die Unterhandlungen abgebrochen und
zwar in der Weise, daß „Standard, das Organ des
torystischen Kabinets, des Bestimmtesten erklärte, der
neue englische Minister in Washington habe sein Ohr
jedem weitern Vorschlagüber die Alabamafrage zu ver
schließen. Bei der zwischen beiden Kabineten herrschenden
Spannung, die durch den für amerikanische Bürger in
Europa verlangten Schutz noch höher geschraubt wird, ist
es sich daher nicht zu verwundern, wenn es nächstens zu
Noten oder zu einem Ultimatum käme.
Die Eisenbahnen der Vereinigten Staaten von Nord
amerika umfassen gegenwärtig eine Länge von 38,605
englischen Meilen. Die Erstellung, derselben kostete
1,654,050,799 Dollars.
In Wafhington ist der offizielle Bericht angelangt,
daß die Zession der Insel St. Thomas in Kopenhagen
ratifizirt worden sei.
Mehrere Söhne der ersten Familien des Königreichs
Siam sind in Paris erwartet.
Nach glaubwürdigen Londoner Privatberichten treten
die erfreulichsten Vorzeichen eines kräftigern Geschäfts
verkehrs zu Tage. Diese Erscheinung ist um so tröst
licher, als die industrielle Krise von 1866 in England
zugleich mit einer schlechten Ernte und einer großen
Theuerung der Nahrungsmittel verbunden war.
Der Widerspruch gegen das von Disraeli vorgeschla
gene Wahlbestechungsgericht — drei Richter mit je einem
Gehalt von 200 Pfund — erklärt sich aus der Be
schränkung, die dadurch den Rechten des Unterhauses
erwachsen wäre. Bis jetzt unterlag nämlich der Fall
dem Urtheil der Gemeinen oder der von diesen gewählten
Kommission.
Im ungarischen Comitat Zips, das an Galizien
grenzt, ist man auf Verzweigungen einer ausgedehnten
panslavistischen Agitation gestoßen. Die Regierung hat
eine Untersuchung angeordnet. Der Direktor des Ly
ceums von Leutschau ist schwer kompromittirt. Monat
lich werden jetzt 50,000 umgeänderte Gewehre an die
Armee abgeliefert.
In Oesterreich werden sämmtliche zur Umänderung
in Hinterlader geeignete Gewehre, deren Zahl ungefähr
600,000 Stück beträgt, bis zu Ende des Jahres umge
ändert sein.
Der Streit über die Hannoveraner Emigration ist
in den gestrigen telegraphischen Depeschen nach allen
Seiten auseinandergesetzt worden. Von ganz besonderer
Bedeutung ist die letzten Samstag in der N. Z. Ztg.
erschienene Bundesstadt-Korrespondenz, durch welche die
Angabe des Lieutenant v. Tschirschnitz, als ob die Han
noveraner durch preußischen Einfluß aus der Schweiz
verdrängt worden seien, als durch und durch unbegrün
det nachgewiesen wird.
Der Antrag des Deputirten Mellana, das Militär
büdget von 162 Millionen auf 142 zu reduziren, wurde
verworfen.
Der „Pungolo" von Mailand spricht von einem Ar
beiter, der mit 40,000 Fr. in Gold, dem Verdienst meh
rerer Jahre, aus Amerika nach Varese zurückgekehrt ist
und seine Baarschaft in Bankbillets (45,000 Fr.) um
gewechselt hat. Dieses Papier nun sei in einer unglück
lichen Viertelstunde durch ein Kind von dem Tische, auf
welchem es ausgebreitet war, weggetragen und in's Ka
minfeuer geworfen worden. Der unglückliche Arbeiter
sei über den Schlag in eine solche Wuth gerathen, daß
er dem kleinen Anstifter seines Unglücks einen Fußtritt
versetzte, welcher den Tod nach sich zog. Der doppelt
Unglückliche sei bereits vor Gericht gestellt.
Laut belgischen Korrespondenzen ist die Arbeiter
Bewegung, wie sie diesen Augenblick im Hennegau auf
getreten ist, eine Erscheinung, die so regelmäßig eintritt
als der Winter und die mit demselben verbundene Ab
nahme des Verdienstes. Leider wird der seit einem Vier
teljahrhundert sich alljährlich erneuernde Kampf zwischen
der Polizei und den Arbeitern der Kohlenbergwerke von
Jahr zu Jahr blutiger und dürfte am Ende zu einer
schrecklichen Katastrophe führen.
Was von einem parlamentarischen Ministerium in
Frankreich verlautet hat, ist durch den gestrigen Pariser
Telegraphen total in Abrede gestellt worden.
Der vor Kurzem verstorbene Senator Montlaville
war ein geschworner Feind der Engländer ganz à la
Marquis Boissy. Von ihm kursirte die Bitte an den
Kaiser in Bordeaux: Sire, ich hoffe, daß Sie mich noch
einmal zum Präfekten von London wählen.
Abbe Migne's Druckerei der Kirchenväter in Paris ist
abgebrannt. Der Schaden wird auf 6 Mill. angeschlagen
und ist so versichert.
Heute Abends, 5 Uhr 21 Minuten, von Sonnen
untergang an bis zum Verschwinden des Jupiters, 7 Uhr
Abends, sieht man, wenn das Wetter günstig, über dem
letztern Gestirn einen kleinen röthlichen Stern, nämlich
den Planeten Merkur, welcher der Sonne dreimal näher
ist als die Erde. Seit tausend Jahren befand sich der
Merkur in keiner für unsere Beobachtung so günstigen
Stellung: Einerseits steht der Mond nicht über dem
Horizont, anderseits bildet der Jupiter einen Abstandspunkt
und dieses gerade in dem Augenblick, wo der Merkur
sich in der größtmöglichen östlichen Entfernung von der
Sonne befindet. Bekanntlich hat der Astronom Gassendi
noch auf dem Todbette sein Bedauern ausgesprochen, daß
ihm das Glück nicht geworden sei, den Merkur von freiem
Auge zu sehen.

completion:
Night Review.

The Alabama Claims, which are increasingly coming to the forefront, consist of two demands. First, compensation is demanded from North America for the Northern merchant ships that were captured and burned by corsairs such as the Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Sumter, etc., which were purchased and armed in England during the Civil War. Secondly, England is also accused of violating international law by allowing the outfitting of Confederate privateers in its ports. From Washington, arbitration on both issues was proposed, while England was willing to submit to arbitration on the first issue but refuses to tolerate any intervention in its internal maritime policy. Since the United States did not want to separate the two points, negotiations were broken off, and in such a way that the *Standard*, the organ of the Tory cabinet, declared most decisively that the new English minister in Washington should close his ears to any further proposals regarding the Alabama Claims. Given the tension between the two cabinets, which is further heightened by the protection demanded for American citizens in Europe, it is therefore not surprising if it soon comes to diplomatic notes or an ultimatum.

The railways of the United States of North America currently span a length of 38,605 English miles. Their construction cost 1,654,050,799 dollars.

In Washington, the official report has arrived that the cession of the island of St. Thomas has been ratified in Copenhagen.

Several sons of the first families of the Kingdom of Siam are expected in Paris.

According to reliable private reports from London, the most favorable signs of stronger business activity are emerging. This phenomenon is all the more comforting as the industrial crisis of 1866 in England coincided with a poor harvest and a great increase in the cost of food.

The opposition to the election bribery court proposed by Disraeli—three judges with a salary of 200 pounds each—is explained by the limitation that would thereby be imposed on the rights of the House of Commons. Until now, such cases were subject to the judgment of the Commons or a commission elected by them.

In the Hungarian county of Zips, which borders Galicia, evidence of an extensive Pan-Slavic agitation has been uncovered. The government has ordered an investigation. The director of the Lyceum in Leutschau is seriously compromised. Currently, 50,000 converted rifles are being delivered to the army monthly.

In Austria, all rifles suitable for conversion into breech-loaders, numbering approximately 600,000, will be converted by the end of the year.

The dispute over the Hanoverian emigration has been explained from all sides in yesterday's telegraphic dispatches. Of particular significance is the federal city correspondence published last Saturday in the *Neue Zürcher Zeitung*, which proves that Lieutenant von Tschirschnitz's claim, as if the Hanoverians had been expelled from Switzerland by Prussian influence, is entirely unfounded.

The motion by Deputy Mellana to reduce the military budget from 162 million to 142 million was rejected.

The *Pungolo* of Milan speaks of a worker who returned from America to Varese with 40,000 francs in gold, the earnings of several years, and exchanged his cash for banknotes (45,000 francs). This paper was then, in an unfortunate quarter of an hour, carried away from the table on which it was spread out by a child and thrown into the fireplace. The unfortunate worker became so enraged by the blow that he kicked the little instigator of his misfortune, resulting in death. The doubly unfortunate man has already been brought to court.

According to Belgian correspondences, the workers' movement, as it has appeared at this moment in Hainaut, is a phenomenon that occurs as regularly as winter and the associated decrease in earnings. Unfortunately, the conflict between the police and the coal miners, which has been renewed annually for a quarter of a century, is becoming bloodier year by year and may ultimately lead to a terrible catastrophe.

The rumors about a parliamentary ministry in France have been completely denied by yesterday's Paris telegraph.

The recently deceased Senator Montlaville was a sworn enemy of the English, quite in the style of Marquis Boissy. A request attributed to him circulated to the Emperor in Bordeaux: "Sire, I hope that you will once again appoint me as Prefect of London."

Abbé Migne's printing house of the Church Fathers in Paris has burned down. The damage is estimated at 6 million and is insured as such.

This evening, from 5:21 p.m., starting at sunset until Jupiter disappears at 7 p.m., if the weather is favorable, one can see a small reddish star above the latter planet, namely the planet Mercury, which is three times closer to the Sun than Earth. For a thousand years, Mercury has not been in such a favorable position for our observation: on one hand, the Moon is not above the horizon; on the other, Jupiter serves as a reference point, and this precisely at the moment when Mercury is at its greatest possible eastern distance from the Sun. It is well known that the astronomer Gassendi expressed regret on his deathbed that he had not been fortunate enough to see Mercury with the naked eye.

einmal zum Präfekten von London wählen.

abgebrannt. Der Schaden wird auf 6 Mill. angeschlagen
und ist so versichert.

untergang an bis zum Verschwinden des Jupiters, 7 Uhr

letztern Gestirn einen kleinen röthlichen Stern, nämlich

sich in der größtmöglichen östlichen Entfernung von der

First, compensation is demanded from North America for the Northern merchant ships that were captured and burned by corsairs such as the Alabama, Georgia, Florida, Sumter, etc., which were purchased and armed in England during the Civil War. Secondly, England is also accused of violating international law by allowing the outfitting of Confederate privateers in its ports. From Washington, arbitration on both issues was proposed, while England was willing to submit to arbitration on the first issue but refuses to tolerate any intervention in its internal maritime policy. Since the United States did not want to separate the two points, negotiations were broken off, and in such a way that the *Standard*, the organ of the Tory cabinet, declared most decisively that the new English minister in Washington should close his ears to any further proposals regarding the Alabama Claims. The railways of the United States of North America currently span a length of 38,605 English miles. Their construction cost 1,654,050,799 dollars.

In Washington, the official report has arrived that the cession of the island of St. Thomas has been ratified in Copenhagen.

Several sons of the first families of the Kingdom of Siam are expected in Paris.

According to reliable private reports from London, the most favorable signs of stronger business activity are emerging. This phenomenon is all the more comforting as the industrial crisis of 1866 in England coincided with a poor harvest and a great increase in the cost of food.

The opposition to the election bribery court proposed by Disraeli—three judges with a salary of 200 pounds each—is explained by the limitation that would thereby be imposed on the rights of the House of Commons. In the Hungarian county of Zips, which borders Galicia, evidence of an extensive Pan-Slavic agitation has been uncovered. The government has ordered an investigation. In Austria, all rifles suitable for conversion into breech-loaders, numbering approximately 600,000, will be converted by the end of the year.

The dispute over the Hanoverian emigration has been explained from all sides in yesterday's telegraphic dispatches. Of particular significance is the federal city correspondence published last Saturday in the *Neue Zürcher Zeitung*, which proves that Lieutenant von Tschirschnitz's claim, as if the Hanoverians had been expelled from Switzerland by Prussian influence, is entirely unfounded.

The motion by Deputy Mellana to reduce the military budget from 162 million to 142 million was rejected.

The *Pungolo* of Milan speaks of a worker who returned from America to Varese with 40,000 francs in gold, the earnings of several years, and exchanged his cash for banknotes (45,000 francs). This paper was then, in an unfortunate quarter of an hour, carried away from the table on which it was spread out by a child and thrown into the fireplace. The unfortunate worker became so enraged by the blow that he kicked the little instigator of his misfortune, resulting in death. The doubly unfortunate man has already been brought to court.

According to Belgian correspondences, the workers' movement, as it has appeared at this moment in Hainaut, is a phenomenon that occurs as regularly as winter and the associated decrease in earnings. Unfortunately, the conflict between the police and the coal miners, which has been renewed annually for a quarter of a century, is becoming bloodier year by year and may ultimately lead to a terrible catastrophe.

The rumors about a parliamentary ministry in France have been completely denied by yesterday's Paris telegraph.

The recently deceased Senator Montlaville was a sworn enemy of the English, quite in the style of Marquis Boissy. A request attributed to him circulated to the Emperor in Bordeaux: "Sire, I hope that you will once again appoint me as Prefect of London."

Abbé Migne's printing house of the Church Fathers in Paris has burned down. The damage is estimated at 6 million and is insured as such.

This evening, from 5:21 p.m., starting at sunset until Jupiter disappears at 7 p.m., if the weather is favorable, one can see a small reddish star above the latter planet, namely the planet Mercury, which is three times closer to the Sun than Earth. For a thousand years, Mercury has not been in such a favorable position for our observation: on one hand, the Moon is not above the horizon; on the other, Jupiter serves as a reference point, and this precisely at the moment when Mercury is at its greatest possible eastern distance from the Sun. It is well known that the astronomer Gassendi expressed regret on his deathbed that he had not been fortunate enough to see Mercury with the naked eye.

September 28th has proven that the people of Luxembourg have awakened to freedom and independence, and that a new era has dawned for our country and people. For whom the future of the country belongs can no longer be doubtful to anyone who has attentively observed the events of these days. The immense majority of the Luxembourg people is good, is fundamentally healthy, and is fed up and weary of the regime that has oppressed the people until now. The direction represented in the Luxembourg Word unites all truly conservative elements within itself; there all truly moderate and thoughtful elements are represented, and the people, long kept in immaturity and oppression, have begun to rise to freedom and independence.

The friends of bureaucracy have attempted to portray the Luxembourg Word as the organ of a clerical party. However, it has never represented one-sided clerical principles; it has endeavored to gather and protect all truly conservative elements, and has always considered itself the true bulwark against revolution and social dissolution. Recently, by publishing its electoral lists, it has proven that it does not pursue exclusively clerical aims, but rather strives only to resist the despotism on one side and the anarchism on the other. It has never made common cause with an ambiguous party to achieve an immediate goal, but rather, even spurning momentary advantage, has steadfastly adhered to its unshakeable principles, connecting to the history of a better past, confidently looking forward to the development of a freer and happier future. That the future belongs to us is proven by the outcome of the elections. Almost everywhere, in the first ballot, the candidates nominated by the Luxembourg Central Electoral Committee received the great majority of votes, proof that the great majority of the population is for us. And even though in the second ballot some candidates were lost again, as in Echternach (Gigrang and Dieschburg), in Wiltz (Neumann), in Grevenmacher (Kuborn), nevertheless the overall result of the elections is to be called a pleasing one. In contrast, the party of the government has suffered a decisive defeat almost everywhere, and its main representatives, such as Ledure, Macher, Wellenstein, Lafontaine, Brasseur, etc., mostly failed precisely because they were men of the government. In Nemich, the most decided opposition against the government triumphed completely and most brilliantly. In Esch an der Alzette, the extraordinary efforts of Motte were unable to secure victory for Messrs. Lafontaine and Würth-Paquet. The latter failed even in the ballot against the priest and professor Müller (not to be confused with the director Müller at the Athenaeum) by a large majority of votes. Here, of course, the particular circumstance added that the mission to The Hague had greatly damaged the popularity of the mild candidate. In Luxembourg itself, the party of the government, represented primarily by Simonis, did not even emerge. At the decisive moment, it had thrown itself into the arms of Metz's party and offered it every support to thwart the otherwise undoubtedly already secure victory of the Catholic Electoral Committee. By this, it indeed succeeded in excluding the most respectable citizens of the city, who have rendered the most disinterested services to their fellow citizens for many years, from the elections, and bringing a series of completely insignificant and unknown men into the election; but hardly has it thereby earned the gratitude of the citizenry, which is not indifferent to the honor of the city. Nevertheless, in the Canton of Luxembourg, the Catholic Electoral Committee would have carried off the victory on September 28th, if several hundred votes had not been wrested from the Catholic voters in the most violent manner. On the side of the opponents, a multitude of bailiffs, secretaries, mayors, and other servile people were active. People were forced to show their ballots, they were torn from them by force, others were pressed upon them, or false ballots were substituted, on which only the first name of the other electoral list stood. In this manner, one even saw a clerk and other officials extremely active. Against this swarm of official helpers, the Catholic Electoral Committee had for its aid only the core of the middle-class citizenry of the city. The citizenry, however, took up the cause with an zeal, an effort, and a devotion that cannot be sufficiently acknowledged and praised. It is a splendid, robust spirit in our citizenry that justifies the fairest hopes for the future. Through the zeal of the citizens, the two election bureaus in the city hall and the two in the Athenaeum were monitored, and the voters from the countryside were protected. At all four bureaus, therefore, the outcome of the elections was also very satisfactory. But at the two bureaus in the Tribunal, every access for the Catholic citizens was forcibly cut off, while people who were not even voters freely went in and out. There the voters were without any protection from their like-minded peers, and thus alone here more than 150 votes were lost. These two bureaus decided the preponderance of the other electoral list.

It has risen to such strength only through its inner power and has united all conservative and morally sound elements within itself. It has appeared for the first time formally on the battlefield of elections, and it required the unification of all other parties and the application of all and every means, which perhaps will not be available to them for long anymore, to secure its victory. We are completely satisfied with this development of our circumstances and look toward the future with confidence.

klerikalen Partei auswusch reien. Dasselbe hat aber nie
einseitige klerikale Prinzipien vertreten, es hat alle
wahrhaft conservativcn Elemente zu sammeln und
zu beschützen sich bemüht, und sich immer als die
eigentliche Sckutzwehr gegen die Revolution und

nächstes Ziel zu erreichen, sondern hat, selbst
augenblicklichen Vorlheil verschmähend festgehalten an fei*
nen unumstößlichen Pnnzipien, anknüpfend an die
Geschichte einer besseren Vergangenheit, der
Entwickelung einer freieren und glücklicheren Zukunft
getrost entgegensehend. Daß die Zukunft für uns

erhielten bei der ersten Abstimmung die vom
Luremburgcr Ccutralwahlcomite aufgestellten
Candidate» die große Mehrheit der Stimmen, ein Beweis,
daß die große Mehrheit der Bevölkerung für uns
ist. Und gingen auch bei der zweiten Abstimmung
manche Candidaten wieder verloren, wie in
Echternach Gigrang und Dieschburg, in Wiltz Neumann,
in Grevenmachern Kuborn, so ist dennoch das
Gesammtrcsultat der Wahlen ein erfreuliches zu
nennen. Dagegen hat die Partei der Regierung fast
überall eine entschiedene Niederlage erlitten, und
ihre Hauptvertreter, wie Ledure, Macher, Wellenstein,
Lafontaine, Brasseur u. a. sielen meistens gerabe
deshalb, weil sie Männer der Regierung waren,

Der Wahltag zu Luxemburg.

Nokraschi Pasha
Edition 7. The Egyptian Prime Minister Mahmud Fahmi Al-Nokraschi Pasha, who was murdered in Cairo on Monday, belonged, although he was already 60 years old, to the relatively young politicians who only entered the political arena in the last two decades. A former supporter of the Wafd, like all Egyptian politicians, he first came into prominence as Minister of Transport in the second cabinet of Nahas Pasha, which remained in office only from January to June 1930. He held the same office again in the third cabinet of Nahas from May 1936. His interesting personality made him particularly popular among the young supporters of the party and also brought him closer to his party friend and age companion Ahmed Maher Pasha, the President of the Chamber of Deputies, from whom he subsequently never separated.

Their parallel career paths began in London, when both were among the thirteen delegates who signed the Anglo-Egyptian treaty in August 1936. After their return to Egypt, they, as younger members of the party, gained the impression that the Wafd had played its last cards in London and thus had no more prospects to offer its supporters. This viewpoint was entirely justified at that time; indeed, the actual decline of the Wafd began at that point. When the Wafd was founded, the sole goal of its program was the conclusion of a treaty with Great Britain that would recognize Egypt's independence. It is known that the Arabic word "Wafd" means nothing other than "delegation." Nahas Pasha had wrested this treaty from the British. The role of the Wafd's "delegation" was thus played out.

In the following months, the leaders of the party, especially Makram Ebeid and to a lesser extent Nahas, behaved as if they now had a right to the country's gratitude. Waste of public funds, corruption, and favoritism became widespread. It seemed as if every hope had been abandoned of ever coming to power again later.

In August 1937, the two friends Maher and Nokraschi broke away from the Wafd and jointly founded a new party, which they named the Saadist Party after the founder of the Wafd, Saad Zaghloul, under the pretext that the party founded by him had not remained true to his spirit. The beginnings were difficult. However, the new party eventually prevailed, and when in August 1939 Ali Maher Pasha, Ahmed's brother, needed their support in forming a new cabinet, he offered their president, Nokraschi, the Ministry of Education.

In June 1940, Ali Maher had to resign due to his pro-German leanings under pressure from the British embassy, and Nokraschi was taken over by the cabinet of Hassan-Sabri Pasha as Minister of Interior. This extremely important office in wartime could undoubtedly only be entrusted to him in agreement with the English.

The Sabri cabinet remained in power only two months. During the opening of parliament, the prime minister was struck by a heart attack while reading the throne speech. His successor Hussein Sirry dispensed with the participation of the Saadists. In February 1942, the Hussein Sirry cabinet was replaced by the last Wafd cabinet under Nahas Pasha. When in October 1944 Lord Killearn and the British government finally had to realize that Nahas Pasha's continued presence in the government endangered their own position, they withdrew their support from him and pressed for the appointment of Ahmed Maher Pasha as successor, who as Nahas' opponent and a pro-British-minded politician was equally well-regarded in the palace and at the British embassy. The two Saadist leaders had thus reached the highest level; they divided the key positions among themselves. Maher kept the Ministry of Interior for himself, and Nokraschi became Minister of Foreign Affairs. Thus he completed the second grade of the "prime minister school," for it has almost become tradition in Egypt that the prime minister, unless he reaches his post via the presidency of the Senate or the Chamber, must have administered one of the three main ministries, namely Interior, Foreign Affairs, or Finance.

Under Ahmed Maher's leadership, Egyptian policy was steered into British waters. This policy cost Maher his life after only a few months. Maher Pasha was shot on February 24, 1945 by a Canadian nationalist, just as he had announced to parliament Egypt's declaration of war on the Axis powers. For Nokraschi, under such circumstances, it was a difficult task to take over his friend's succession. After the war, nationalism intensified in Egypt, which Nokraschi attempted to oppose. As a realist politician who understood how to accurately assess the power resources of his country, he believed that through friendship he could wrest concessions from the British that they would never grant to declared enemies. Personally, Nokraschi would have gladly avoided a revision of the London treaty, clearly aware that stipulations and clauses only have value if one can compel the partner to fulfill its obligations through appropriate means. However, he had to submit to the pressure of the "Eighteen," an advisory committee that the king had established. When he wanted to begin negotiations with London, his government had to yield to the intrigues of the opposition. Nokraschi lacked the necessary self-control and calm. This also showed when in February 1946 he ordered the police to ruthlessly shoot at unarmed student crowds who wanted to cross the Abbas Bridge into the government quarter. His brutal action betrayed not energy, but rather fear.

After Nokraschi Pasha's resignation on February 15, 1946, Ismail Sidky Pasha took over the cabinet, which was supported by Nokraschi, but already had to resign again in December, after which Nokraschi Pasha was reappointed as prime minister on December 10, 1946.

The Burial of Nokraschi Pasha
Cairo, December 29. (AP) The national funeral of Prime Minister Nokraschi Pasha took place on Wednesday morning in Cairo. The funeral procession passed through the city center to a mosque, where a service was held. Then the transfer of the body to the mausoleum, which is being built for the former Prime Minister Ahmed Maher Pasha, who was also murdered in February 1945, followed. The inauguration of the mausoleum was supposed to take place shortly. The body of Ahmed Maher Pasha was brought there during the night so that the two friends and comrades could rest side by side.

The press points to the parallel careers of these two statesmen, who always worked for national liberation, both had to endure exile and prison, and finally were murdered in office as prime ministers by young fanatics.

Statements of the Murderer
Cairo, December 29. (AFP) The murderer of Nokraschi Pasha explained during interrogation that the assassination represented a protest against the policy of the prime minister. (Ban on the "Muslim Brotherhood," policy in Sudan and Palestine.) The murderer is the son of a former official of the Ministry of Interior; he has belonged to the organization of the "Muslim Brotherhood" for several years. His studies at the Veterinary Medical Faculty were made possible by a scholarship that had been granted to him personally by Nokraschi Pasha.

In a drawer of the murdered prime minister's desk, a stack of threatening letters that Nokraschi Pasha had received and about which he had not even ordered an investigation was found.

Since in Egypt martial law prevails since the outbreak of the war with Palestine, the murderer will be sentenced by a military court.

präbnis von Ministerprüsident Nokraschi Paschn
kand am Mittwoelvormittag in Eniro stutt. Der
Tranerzug führte dureh die Stadtmitte unch einer
Mloschee, vo der Gottesdienst abgehalten wurde.
Dann erkolgte die Ueberkührung der Leiche unch
dem Alausokeum, dus für den früheren Minister
prüsidenten Ahmed Maher Pascha erlmut wird, der
im Februar 1945 ebenkulls ermordet worden war.

stattkinden sollen. Die Leiche von Almed Anher
Paselm wurde in der Aneht dorthin gebrucht, dumit
die beiden Freunde und Kampkkamernden Seite an
Seite ruhen können.
Die Presse verweist auf die gleiehurtige lnuk
bahn dieser beiden Stantsminner, die stets für die
nationale Bekreiung arbeiteten, beide Eril und Ge
küngnis erdulden mutten und schlieblieb im Amt
nls Ministerprüsidenten von jungen Fanntikern er
mordet wurden.

schi Pasehas erklärte beim Verhör, das Attentat
stelle einen Protest gegen die Politike des Minister
prüsidenten dar. (Verbot der „Mohammedanischen
Prüdler", Politik im Sudan und in Paliistina.) Der

Nokraschi Pasha
Edition 7. The Egyptian Prime Minister Mahmud Fahmi Al-Nokraschi Pasha, who was murdered in Cairo on Monday, belonged, although he was already 60 years old, to the relatively young politicians who only entered the political arena in the last two decades. A former supporter of the Wafd, like all Egyptian politicians, he first came into prominence as Minister of Transport in the second cabinet of Nahas Pasha, which remained in office only from January to June 1930. He held the same office again in the third cabinet of Nahas from May 1936. His interesting personality made him particularly popular among the young supporters of the party and also brought him closer to his party friend and age companion Ahmed Maher Pasha, the President of the Chamber of Deputies, from whom he subsequently never separated.

Their parallel career paths began in London, when both were among the thirteen delegates who signed the Anglo-Egyptian treaty in August 1936. After their return to Egypt, they, as younger members of the party, gained the impression that the Wafd had played its last cards in London and thus had no more prospects to offer its supporters. This viewpoint was entirely justified at that time; indeed, the actual decline of the Wafd began at that point. When the Wafd was founded, the sole goal of its program was the conclusion of a treaty with Great Britain that would recognize Egypt's independence. It is known that the Arabic word "Wafd" means nothing other than "delegation." Nahas Pasha had wrested this treaty from the British. The role of the Wafd's "delegation" was thus played out.

In the following months, the leaders of the party, especially Makram Ebeid and to a lesser extent Nahas, behaved as if they now had a right to the country's gratitude. Waste of public funds, corruption, and favoritism became widespread. It seemed as if every hope had been abandoned of ever coming to power again later.

In August 1937, the two friends Maher and Nokraschi broke away from the Wafd and jointly founded a new party, which they named the Saadist Party after the founder of the Wafd, Saad Zaghloul, under the pretext that the party founded by him had not remained true to his spirit. The beginnings were difficult. However, the new party eventually prevailed, and when in August 1939 Ali Maher Pasha, Ahmed's brother, needed their support in forming a new cabinet, he offered their president, Nokraschi, the Ministry of Education.

In June 1940, Ali Maher had to resign due to his pro-German leanings under pressure from the British embassy, and Nokraschi was taken over by the cabinet of Hassan-Sabri Pasha as Minister of Interior. This extremely important office in wartime could undoubtedly only be entrusted to him in agreement with the English.

The Sabri cabinet remained in power only two months. During the opening of parliament, the prime minister was struck by a heart attack while reading the throne speech. His successor Hussein Sirry dispensed with the participation of the Saadists. In February 1942, the Hussein Sirry cabinet was replaced by the last Wafd cabinet under Nahas Pasha. When in October 1944 Lord Killearn and the British government finally had to realize that Nahas Pasha's continued presence in the government endangered their own position, they withdrew their support from him and pressed for the appointment of Ahmed Maher Pasha as successor, who as Nahas' opponent and a pro-British-minded politician was equally well-regarded in the palace and at the British embassy. The two Saadist leaders had thus reached the highest level; they divided the key positions among themselves. Maher kept the Ministry of Interior for himself, and Nokraschi became Minister of Foreign Affairs. Thus he completed the second grade of the "prime minister school," for it has almost become tradition in Egypt that the prime minister, unless he reaches his post via the presidency of the Senate or the Chamber, must have administered one of the three main ministries, namely Interior, Foreign Affairs, or Finance.

Under Ahmed Maher's leadership, Egyptian policy was steered into British waters. This policy cost Maher his life after only a few months. Maher Pasha was shot on February 24, 1945 by a Canadian nationalist, just as he had announced to parliament Egypt's declaration of war on the Axis powers. For Nokraschi, under such circumstances, it was a difficult task to take over his friend's succession. After the war, nationalism intensified in Egypt, which Nokraschi attempted to oppose. As a realist politician who understood how to accurately assess the power resources of his country, he believed that through friendship he could wrest concessions from the British that they would never grant to declared enemies. Personally, Nokraschi would have gladly avoided a revision of the London treaty, clearly aware that stipulations and clauses only have value if one can compel the partner to fulfill its obligations through appropriate means. However, he had to submit to the pressure of the "Eighteen," an advisory committee that the king had established. When he wanted to begin negotiations with London, his government had to yield to the intrigues of the opposition. Nokraschi lacked the necessary self-control and calm. This also showed when in February 1946 he ordered the police to ruthlessly shoot at unarmed student crowds who wanted to cross the Abbas Bridge into the government quarter. His brutal action betrayed not energy, but rather fear.

After Nokraschi Pasha's resignation on February 15, 1946, Ismail Sidky Pasha took over the cabinet, which was supported by Nokraschi, but already had to resign again in December, after which Nokraschi Pasha was reappointed as prime minister on December 10, 1946.

The Burial of Nokraschi Pasha
Cairo, December 29. (AP) The national funeral of Prime Minister Nokraschi Pasha took place on Wednesday morning in Cairo. The funeral procession passed through the city center to a mosque, where a service was held. Then the transfer of the body to the mausoleum, which is being built for the former Prime Minister Ahmed Maher Pasha, who was also murdered in February 1945, followed. The inauguration of the mausoleum was supposed to take place shortly. The body of Ahmed Maher Pasha was brought there during the night so that the two friends and comrades could rest side by side.

The press points to the parallel careers of these two statesmen, who always worked for national liberation, both had to endure exile and prison, and finally were murdered in office as prime ministers by young fanatics.

Statements of the Murderer
Cairo, December 29. (AFP) The murderer of Nokraschi Pasha explained during interrogation that the assassination represented a protest against the policy of the prime minister. (Ban on the "Muslim Brotherhood," policy in Sudan and Palestine.) The murderer is the son of a former official of the Ministry of Interior; he has belonged to the organization of the "Muslim Brotherhood" for several years. His studies at the Veterinary Medical Faculty were made possible by a scholarship that had been granted to him personally by Nokraschi Pasha.

In a drawer of the murdered prime minister's desk, a stack of threatening letters that Nokraschi Pasha had received and about which he had not even ordered an investigation was found.

Since in Egypt martial law prevails since the outbreak of the war with Palestine, the murderer will be sentenced by a military court.

Feuilleton.
Erster Lesezirkelabend.
t. Im Theatersaal zur „Kaufleuten" setzten
am Samstag, den 23. November, des Lesezirkels
Hottingen Abende für Literatur und Kunst ein.
Ein neuer Wochentag — statt des zu traulicher
Gewohnheit gewordenen Montag — und ein an
deres Lokal, mit dem man auch erst näher Füh
lung nehmen muß, obschon es an sich durchaus
kein ästhetisches Minus bedeutet. Freilich das nie
dere Podium wird für den Kontakt mit dem Audi
torium immer der höher gelegenen Bühne vorzu
ziehen sein, und das Singen und Sagen direkt vor
dem Vorhang ist akustisch auch kein Ideal. Josef
Reinhart, der Solothurner Dichter, stellte sich
nicht gleich von Anfang an auf die wünsch
bare Tonstärke ein, wozu freilich auch beigetragen
haben mag, daß die Beleuchtungsverhältnisse für
den Vorlesenden nichts weniger als ideale waren.
Aus den stillbehaglichen Geschichten des Bandes
„Waldvogelzyt", in dem die Kindheitserinnerung
das Auge hell und beglückt aufschlägt, las er den
reizenden Abschnitt von der ersten Beichte und
dann den vom ersten Stadtbesuch, auf dem Santi
klausmarkt der St. Ursenstadt vor, köstlich einfache,
humorbesonnte und, namentlich die erste Geschichte,
auch psychologisch recht fein gefaßte Stücke, die dem
Vortragenden reichen Beifall eintrugen. Zur
Prosa spendete er dann auch eine Reihe mund
artliche freundlich-sinnige Lyrica, unter denen
man einer Anzahl von Reinharts besten Sachen
begegnete, u. a. dem Kirchhofgedicht mit der Ge
denkdran-Mahnung, daß kein Toter mehr zurück
kommt. Der Dichter ist seinen Schöpfungen ein
trefflicher Interpret, namentlich die Prosa ersteht
zu ungemein lebendiger Anschaulichkeit.
Dem literarischen Programm dieses ersten
Lesezirkel-Abends waren am Schluß der beiden
durch eine kurze Pause voneinander getrennten
Vorlesungen Joseph Reinharts noch je vier seiner
Dialektlieder in der Vertonung von Fritz
Niggli angefügt. Mit sympathischer Sopran
stimme trug sie Frau Gysin-Mohler vor,
sekundiert am Flügel durch den zuverlässigsten
Begleiter, den man sich wünschen konnte, durch
den Komponisten selbst.
Zu Gehör kamen: „J bien-en arme Fischer",
„Heimliche Liebe", „J möcht e Jeger finde"
„D'Liebi", ferner „Stärnli überm Huns", „Nach
dem Regen", „Rosenzeit" und „Was brucht e rächte
Schwyzerma?" Daß wir in Fritz Niggli ein star
kes Talent gerade zur Liederkomposition besitzen,
darf auch nach den hier gebotenen Proben ohne
Umschweife gern festgestellt werden. Erfreut man
sich bei Josef Reinhart an der dialektischen Klein
kunst, so bei unserm Tondichter an der sie mit
einem Zaubergespinst überwebenden Feinkunst.
Aber, obschon sich über ästhetische Glaubens
bekenntnisse nicht streiten, und noch weniger rech
ten läßt, wollen wir doch kein Hehl aus unserer
persönlichen Empfindung machen, daß die Dia
lektdichtung Reinharts sich gegen eigentlich tra
gische Klänge ihrem innersten Wesen nach ab
lehnend verhält. Der arme Fischer hat seinen
Bettlerhumor nicht so völlig verloren, wie die
Musik allein uns glauben machen könnte. Schubert
mit den elegischen Gesängen seines Müllerlieder
zyklus kam uns, was die Analogie des Stim
mungsgehaltes betrifft, in den Sinn. Auch die
vielsache Verwendung von leiterfremden Tönen
macht einen gewissen Zwiespalt zu dem volks
tümlichen Sprachcharakter der Gedichte gelegent
lich fühlbar. So in der zweiten Zeile von „Stärnli
überm Huns": Ob d'Sunne hinder d'Bärge goht,
so blibt sie nomols stoh". Durchaus bewußt künst
lerisch gewählt war in dem Liedchen „D'Liebi"
die Harmoniefolge zu den Worten: „Und wenns
die gfährligst Chranket wär". Der Hörer sollte sich
hin und her gerüttelt fühlen und doch merken, wie
er sich schließlich wieder zurechtfand. Der
artige Wendungen zeugen von großem Geschick
des Tonsatzes, aber ob sie als volkstümliche gelten
können? Schon die Durchkomposition an sich weist
in die Richtung des hohen Kunstliedes. Deshalb
möchten wir das mit gutem Grund als Nr. 8 an
den Schluß gestellte: „Was brucht e rächte Schwy
zerma?", für einen eigentlichen Treffer halten,
und zwar auch in dem Gesangspart neben der
glänzenden Lust sprühenden Klavierbegleitung
oder besser: Klavierausmalung. Denn auch der
Pianist regt sich lebhaft in der Liederkomposition
Nigglis, tritt also nicht etwa zugunsten eines
dichterischen Vorwurfs in den Hintergrund. Die
Lieder fanden Anklang an dem gutbesuchten Ge
sellschaftsanlaß. Bi.

Feuilleton.
First Reading Circle Evening.
1. On Saturday, November 23, the Hottingen Reading Circle’s Evenings for Literature and Art began in the theater hall of the "Kaufleuten." A new weekday—instead of the Monday that had become a cozy habit—and a different venue, with which one must first become more familiar, although in itself it is by no means an aesthetic drawback. Admittedly, the lower podium will always be preferable to the higher stage for contact with the audience, and singing and speaking directly in front of the curtain is acoustically not ideal either. Josef Reinhart, the poet from Solothurn, did not immediately adjust to the desired volume from the start, which may also have been contributed to by the fact that the lighting conditions for the reader were far from ideal. From the quietly charming stories in the volume "Waldvogelzyt," in which childhood memories open the eye brightly and joyfully, he read the delightful passage about the first confession and then the one about the first visit to the city, at the St. Nicholas market in the city of St. Ursen—exquisitely simple, sunlit with humor, and, especially the first story, also psychologically finely crafted pieces, which earned the performer rich applause. After the prose, he also offered a series of friendly, thoughtful lyrics in dialect, among which one encountered a number of Reinhart's best works, including the cemetery poem with the memorial reminder that no dead person ever returns. The poet is an excellent interpreter of his own creations, especially the prose, which comes to life with extraordinary vividness.

At the end of the two readings by Josef Reinhart, separated by a short intermission, four of his dialect songs each, set to music by Fritz Niggli, were added to the literary program of this first Reading Circle evening. They were performed by Mrs. Gysin-Mohler with a sympathetic soprano voice, accompanied at the piano by the most reliable accompanist one could wish for—the composer himself.

The pieces performed were: "The Poor Fisherman," "Secret Love," "I Wish I Could Find a Hunter," "Love," followed by "Little Stars Above the House," "After the Rain," "Rose Time," and "What Does a True Swiss Man Need?" That we possess in Fritz Niggli a strong talent precisely for song composition can gladly be stated without hesitation, even based on the samples offered here. While one delights in Josef Reinhart's dialect minor art, in our tone poet one delights in the fine art that overlays it with a magical web. But, although one should not argue over aesthetic creeds, and even less dispute them, we do not wish to conceal our personal feeling that Reinhart's dialect poetry, by its innermost nature, resists truly tragic sounds. The poor fisherman has not lost his beggar's humor as completely as the music alone might lead us to believe. Schubert, with the elegiac songs of his Müllerlieder cycle, came to mind in terms of the analogy of emotional content. Also, the frequent use of non-diatonic tones occasionally makes a certain discord with the folk-like linguistic character of the poems palpable. As in the second line of "Little Stars Above the House": "Even if the sun goes behind the mountains, it still remains standing." In the little song "Love," the harmonic progression for the words: "And even if it were the most dangerous illness" was consciously chosen artistically. The listener was meant to feel shaken back and forth and yet notice how they eventually found their way back. Such turns of phrase testify to great skill in composition, but can they be considered folk-like? The through-composition itself points in the direction of the high art song. Therefore, we would consider the piece placed with good reason as No. 8 at the end: "What Does a True Swiss Man Need?" to be a real hit, and indeed also in the vocal part alongside the brilliant, joy-sparkling piano accompaniment—or rather, piano elaboration. For the pianist also stirs vividly in Niggli's song compositions, thus not receding into the background in favor of a poetic subject. The songs were well received at the well-attended social occasion. Bi.

First Reading Circle Evening.
1. On Saturday, November 23, the Hottingen Reading Circle’s Evenings for Literature and Art began in the theater hall of the "Kaufleuten." A new weekday—instead of the Monday that had become a cozy habit—and a different venue, with which one must first become more familiar, although in itself it is by no means an aesthetic drawback. Admittedly, the lower podium will always be preferable to the higher stage for contact with the audience, and singing and speaking directly in front of the curtain is acoustically not ideal either. Josef Reinhart, the poet from Solothurn, did not immediately adjust to the desired volume from the start, which may also have been contributed to by the fact that the lighting conditions for the reader were far from ideal. From the quietly charming stories in the volume "Waldvogelzyt," in which childhood memories open the eye brightly and joyfully, he read the delightful passage about the first confession and then the one about the first visit to the city, at the St. Nicholas market in the city of St. Ursen—exquisitely simple, sunlit with humor, and, especially the first story, also psychologically finely crafted pieces, which earned the performer rich applause. After the prose, he also offered a series of friendly, thoughtful lyrics in dialect, among which one encountered a number of Reinhart's best works, including the cemetery poem with the memorial reminder that no dead person ever returns. The poet is an excellent interpreter of his own creations, especially the prose, which comes to life with extraordinary vividness.

At the end of the two readings by Josef Reinhart, separated by a short intermission, four of his dialect songs each, set to music by Fritz Niggli, were added to the literary program of this first Reading Circle evening. They were performed by Mrs. Gysin-Mohler with a sympathetic soprano voice, accompanied at the piano by the most reliable accompanist one could wish for—the composer himself.

The pieces performed were: "The Poor Fisherman," "Secret Love," "I Wish I Could Find a Hunter," "Love," followed by "Little Stars Above the House," "After the Rain," "Rose Time," and "What Does a True Swiss Man Need?" That we possess in Fritz Niggli a strong talent precisely for song composition can gladly be stated without hesitation, even based on the samples offered here. While one delights in Josef Reinhart's dialect minor art, in our tone poet one delights in the fine art that overlays it with a magical web. But, although one should not argue over aesthetic creeds, and even less dispute them, we do not wish to conceal our personal feeling that Reinhart's dialect poetry, by its innermost nature, resists truly tragic sounds. The poor fisherman has not lost his beggar's humor as completely as the music alone might lead us to believe. Schubert, with the elegiac songs of his Müllerlieder cycle, came to mind in terms of the analogy of emotional content. Also, the frequent use of non-diatonic tones occasionally makes a certain discord with the folk-like linguistic character of the poems palpable. As in the second line of "Little Stars Above the House": "Even if the sun goes behind the mountains, it still remains standing." In the little song "Love," the harmonic progression for the words: "And even if it were the most dangerous illness" was consciously chosen artistically. The listener was meant to feel shaken back and forth and yet notice how they eventually found their way back. Such turns of phrase testify to great skill in composition, but can they be considered folk-like? The through-composition itself points in the direction of the high art song. Therefore, we would consider the piece placed with good reason as No. 8 at the end: "What Does a True Swiss Man Need?" to be a real hit, and indeed also in the vocal part alongside the brilliant, joy-sparkling piano accompaniment—or rather, piano elaboration. Prince Leopold of Coburg was continually detained at Claremont due to his poor health. He received very few visitors and seemed perpetually absorbed in pain.

As is known, Parliament established a committee tasked with deciding on the plans for the British national monuments commemorating the great victories at sea and on land. The plans submitted by the architects—Smirke for the naval power and Wilkins for the land forces—have been approved. The Waterloo Monument will cost £200,000 sterling and will be erected at the end of Portland Place, near the Prince Regent's Park. It will consist of an ancient-style tower with three column orders, around whose base a circular colonnade extends, similar to one of the most admired relics of antiquity, the Temple of the Sibyl at Tivoli. The Trafalgar Column will cost £100,000 and will be erected at Greenwich. It consists of a simple octagon on a suitable base, topped with a naval crown, accessed by colossal steps. Work is underway on both monuments. Additionally, in honor of the Duke of Wellington, a monument will be erected on Blakdown Hill, taking the form of a triangle and reaching a height of 150 feet, crowned with a 20-foot-high statue of the Duke cast in iron. The cost is estimated at £20,000 sterling, and the foundation stone is to be laid by Lord Somerville next year.

**Eighth Issue. Sixth Year. Provincial Correspondence; February 19, 1868.**

**The Provincial Fund in the House of Lords.**

The House of Lords has justified the confidence recently expressed in this place: in the matter of the Hanoverian Provincial Fund, it has placed the viewpoints of a grand patriotic policy above all other considerations and inclinations and has granted the state government its willing and full support for the implementation of its intentions for the new province. More numerous than usual were the members of the House who have declared themselves in favor; those who have declared against did so not against the proposed grant in general, but partly only against its amount and form.

The question, which had so unexpectedly and vividly agitated political circles, has thus been brought to a satisfactory solution through the agreement of the government and both houses of the Landtag: for the provincial needs of Hanover, insofar as they were previously met from general state funds, provision has now also been made by the state, though not, as originally proposed, through the separation of a specific capital, but through the permanent allocation of a fixed annuity. Thus, the benevolent intention of the King for the newly acquired province is fulfilled.

In the earlier discussion of the matter, it was repeatedly emphasized that for the government it was a matter of fulfilling an explicit royal promise given to the Hanoverian estates. This promise referred, of course (as is stressed from another side), initially only to the submission of the draft law to the Landtag. Its fulfillment did not lie solely in the hands of the government, subject to the constant and independent discretion of the national representation; it depended at the same time on the self-evident trust that the government could place in the conservative party, which has hitherto followed the government with full confidence and devotion. In granting that promise, however, the government had to proceed from the confidence that those parties, on which it places particular weight, would rise to the task of serving as a firm support.

Transitory, unjustified doubts about the significance of the affair may have created a momentary uncertainty about its outcome. After the position of the government had been disseminated, after the question had been decisively recognized as one of confidence and agreement with the overall policy of the government, it could no longer be doubtful that the royal promises for Hanover would find willing fulfillment on the part of the national representation.

In such a sense, it has been pointed out on the part of the government, as well as here, to the promise given. The King's expectation has not been disappointed: only against this did the course of the deliberations in the House of Deputies bring full clarity about the intentions and the justice. The government certainly holds the opinion and intention far from "buying the patriotism of the Hanoverians with money"; but it may well hope, through mildness, justice, and brotherly accommodation for the new provinces, to prepare a ground there upon which attachment and patriotic devotion can gradually thrive.

But not only in Hanover, not only in the recently acquired parts of the country is that magnanimous policy appreciated: everywhere in Germany and beyond its borders, the attention and recognition of governments and peoples are directed at Prussia's conduct in the conquered provinces. The most significant voices from South Germany announce just now the powerful impression which the firm stance of the government has spread, with how good reason Count Bismarck pointed out that this Hanoverian question could only be correctly judged in the context of Prussia's overall policy. The policy, which the House of Lords has now also approved, is a policy of benevolence and justice. It proves itself herein, that a state which so carefully preserves the rights and provincial independence of the acquired territories pursues not a narrow-minded policy of conquest, but a truly national policy, and therefore may justly claim the full measure of the German people's trust.

By its latest decision, entering anew with the fullest determination for this policy, the House of Lords has at the same time increased the confidence that the conservative party, which has hitherto followed the government with full trust and devotion, will continue to find its task and its honor in standing willingly by a government which has achieved and created so much for Prussia and Germany, and willingly supporting it also in the fulfillment of the hopes awakened by those promises.

**The So-Called Hanoverian Legion.**

While the Prussian government shows the greatest and noblest consideration to the former King of Hanover, while on the other hand its care for the new province under the blessed cooperation of the greater part of the population prepares the ground there for a prosperous development, the former King George and his entourage in Hietzing have continued the reprehensible attempts to win over a part of his former subjects, mostly from the lowest classes, for the completely hopeless and foolish undertaking of restoring his throne.

Already at the time when the Luxembourg question threatened to bring about a complication between Germany and France, King George had recruitments for a Hanoverian Legion carried out in his former country, which was to assemble in Holland and march in conjunction with the French against their fatherland. When then the Luxembourg affair found a peaceful solution, the gathered troop of Hanoverians went from Holland to Switzerland, where it remained in fixed military division and continually received its sustenance from the funds of King George. Through its idle roaming and its arrogance, it often caused offense there and was not viewed very kindly by the Swiss population as well as by the cantonal governments.

Recently, this so-called "Hanoverian Legion" went from Switzerland to France, where it first took up residence in Alsace, immediately on the German border. However harmless this foolish undertaking is, it had to cause astonishment that an obviously anti-Prussian armed troop of Hanoverian refugees had effected its transfer from Switzerland to France with the help of Austrian passports and that it, as was first said, found accommodating reception on the part of the authorities in France.

The French government has in the meantime for its part taken steps to counter such an interpretation: it has separated the men from the officers and removed the troop from the German border. The Prussian government has no reason to distrust France's friendly intentions regarding the further treatment of the matter. As for Austria, the assurance has been given on the part of its government that the passports for the Hanoverians were issued by the Austrian police authority without the knowledge of the Austrian state government, which, given the large number of passports and the unmistakable political significance of the matter, must in any case appear highly remarkable. The discussions between the Prussian and the Austrian government on this point are still ongoing; it cannot yet be stated with certainty whether and to what extent a violation of international law has occurred in the affair.

But this can hardly be subject to doubt, that the continuation of warlike enterprises against Prussia by a prince who lets Prussian subjects be recruited and armed for a war against Prussia cannot exactly be regarded as a sign of a friendly stance towards Prussia.

Regarding the conduct of King George, the State Minister von der Heydt has just stated in the House of Lords that if his hostile attempts continue, if King George assumes a position that is completely contradictory to the spirit and meaning of the treaty concluded with him—if King George abuses the Austrian hospitality granted to him, the government will then be obliged to take the measures commanded by the duty of self-preservation.

**The Provincial Fund in the House of Lords.**

The House of Lords has justified the confidence recently expressed in this place: in the matter of the Hanoverian Provincial Fund, it has placed the viewpoints of a grand patriotic policy above all other considerations and inclinations and has granted the state government its willing and full support for the implementation of its intentions for the new province. More numerous than usual were the members of the House who have declared themselves in favor; those who have declared against did so not against the proposed grant in general, but partly only against its amount and form.

The question, which had so unexpectedly and vividly agitated political circles, has thus been brought to a satisfactory solution through the agreement of the government and both houses of the Landtag: for the provincial needs of Hanover, insofar as they were previously met from general state funds, provision has now also been made by the state, though not, as originally proposed, through the separation of a specific capital, but through the permanent allocation of a fixed annuity. Thus, the benevolent intention of the King for the newly acquired province is fulfilled.

In the earlier discussion of the matter, it was repeatedly emphasized that for the government it was a matter of fulfilling an explicit royal promise given to the Hanoverian estates. This promise referred, of course (as is stressed from another side), initially only to the submission of the draft law to the Landtag. Its fulfillment did not lie solely in the hands of the government, subject to the constant and independent discretion of the national representation; it depended at the same time on the self-evident trust that the government could place in the conservative party, which has hitherto followed the government with full confidence and devotion. In granting that promise, however, the government had to proceed from the confidence that those parties, on which it places particular weight, would rise to the task of serving as a firm support.

Transitory, unjustified doubts about the significance of the affair may have created a momentary uncertainty about its outcome. After the position of the government had been disseminated, after the question had been decisively recognized as one of confidence and agreement with the overall policy of the government, it could no longer be doubtful that the royal promises for Hanover would find willing fulfillment on the part of the national representation.

In such a sense, it has been pointed out on the part of the government, as well as here, to the promise given. The King's expectation has not been disappointed: only against this did the course of the deliberations in the House of Deputies bring full clarity about the intentions and the justice. The government certainly holds the opinion and intention far from "buying the patriotism of the Hanoverians with money"; but it may well hope, through mildness, justice, and brotherly accommodation for the new provinces, to prepare a ground there upon which attachment and patriotic devotion can gradually thrive.

But not only in Hanover, not only in the recently acquired parts of the country is that magnanimous policy appreciated: everywhere in Germany and beyond its borders, the attention and recognition of governments and peoples are directed at Prussia's conduct in the conquered provinces. The most significant voices from South Germany announce just now the powerful impression which the firm stance of the government has spread, with how good reason Count Bismarck pointed out that this Hanoverian question could only be correctly judged in the context of Prussia's overall policy. The policy, which the House of Lords has now also approved, is a policy of benevolence and justice. It proves itself herein, that a state which so carefully preserves the rights and provincial independence of the acquired territories pursues not a narrow-minded policy of conquest, but a truly national policy, and therefore may justly claim the full measure of the German people's trust.

By its latest decision, entering anew with the fullest determination for this policy, the House of Lords has at the same time increased the confidence that the conservative party, which has hitherto followed the government with full trust and devotion, will continue to find its task and its honor in standing willingly by a government which has achieved and created so much for Prussia and Germany, and willingly supporting it also in the fulfillment of the hopes awakened by those promises.

**The So-Called Hanoverian Legion.**

While the Prussian government shows the greatest and noblest consideration to the former King of Hanover, while on the other hand its care for the new province under the blessed cooperation of the greater part of the population prepares the ground there for a prosperous development, the former King George and his entourage in Hietzing have continued the reprehensible attempts to win over a part of his former subjects, mostly from the lowest classes, for the completely hopeless and foolish undertaking of restoring his throne.

Already at the time when the Luxembourg question threatened to bring about a complication between Germany and France, King George had recruitments for a Hanoverian Legion carried out in his former country, which was to assemble in Holland and march in conjunction with the French against their fatherland. When then the Luxembourg affair found a peaceful solution, the gathered troop of Hanoverians went from Holland to Switzerland, where it remained in fixed military division and continually received its sustenance from the funds of King George. Through its idle roaming and its arrogance, it often caused offense there and was not viewed very kindly by the Swiss population as well as by the cantonal governments.

Recently, this so-called "Hanoverian Legion" went from Switzerland to France, where it first took up residence in Alsace, immediately on the German border. However harmless this foolish undertaking is, it had to cause astonishment that an obviously anti-Prussian armed troop of Hanoverian refugees had effected its transfer from Switzerland to France with the help of Austrian passports and that it, as was first said, found accommodating reception on the part of the authorities in France.

The French government has in the meantime for its part taken steps to counter such an interpretation: it has separated the men from the officers and removed the troop from the German border. The Prussian government has no reason to distrust France's friendly intentions regarding the further treatment of the matter. As for Austria, the assurance has been given on the part of its government that the passports for the Hanoverians were issued by the Austrian police authority without the knowledge of the Austrian state government, which, given the large number of passports and the unmistakable political significance of the matter, must in any case appear highly remarkable. The discussions between the Prussian and the Austrian government on this point are still ongoing; it cannot yet be stated with certainty whether and to what extent a violation of international law has occurred in the affair.

But this can hardly be subject to doubt, that the continuation of warlike enterprises against Prussia by a prince who lets Prussian subjects be recruited and armed for a war against Prussia cannot exactly be regarded as a sign of a friendly stance towards Prussia.

Regarding the conduct of King George, the State Minister von der Heydt has just stated in the House of Lords that if his hostile attempts continue, if King George assumes a position that is completely contradictory to the spirit and meaning of the treaty concluded with him—if King George abuses the Austrian hospitality granted to him, the government will then be obliged to take the measures commanded by the duty of self-preservation.

Tagesbericht
10. a.
Gar eigenartige Gedanken, schreibt unser
Wiener VKorrespondent, sind es, die der soeben
bekannt gewordene, in ganz Ungarn leiden
schaftlich bejubelte Entschluß des Kaisers in
den deutschen, d. h. in den einzigen noch gut
altösterreichischen Kreisen hervorruft.
Dem Fernstehenden mag vielleicht Verständnis
und Gefühl für diese Auslegung der Sache
mangeln. Aber wenn er ihrer Vorgeschichte sich
erinnert, dann wird auch er das Gefühl teilen.
Es handelt sich um folgendes. Sofort nach der
Genfer Unthat, welcher die Kaiserin-Königin
Elisabeth zum Opfer fiel, beschloß man in
Pest, der erhabenen Frau, die als eine besondere
Freundin der Ungarn gegolten hatte, ein wür
diges Denkmal in der ungarischen Hauptstadt zu
errichten. An der Spitze des hiefür gebildeten
Ausschusses steht Ministerpräsident Baron Banffy,
und die im ganzen Lande eingeleiteten Samm
lungen ergaben bisher bereits die hohe Summe
von 400,000 Gulden. Gestern trat der Denkmal
Ausschuß zu einer Sitzung zusammen, inzwelcher
die Stelle beschlossen werden sollte, an welcher
das Denkmal aufzurichten sei. Der Minister
präsident ergriff das Wort zu einer Mit
teilung. Er eröffnete dem Ausschusse,
der „König" habe den Wunsch ausgesprochen,
das Denkmal seiner hohen Gemahlin möge genau
an der Stelle angebracht werden, auf welcher
bisher das Denkmal des Generals Hentzi
steht, der Mitte des schönsten Platzes der Festung
Ofen. Das Hentzi-Denkmal wolle der Kaiser
auf seine Kosten entfernen und auf dem Fried
hofe oder im Innern eines militärischen Gebäudes
wieder aufrichten lassen.
Der Jubel, mit dem diese Anordnung des
Monarchen in Ungarn begrüßt wurde und der
in der Presse in leidenschaftlichen, fast rasenden
Stimmungsergüssen der Dankbarkeit und des
Nationalstolzes sich ausdrückt, gilt natürlich nicht
der ziemlich gleichgültigen Frage, wo das Denk
mal der Kaiserin seinen Platz findet, sondern
dem Umstande, daß das Hentzi-Denkmal beseitigt,
d. h. in irgend einem den Augen der Bevölke
rung fast unzugänglichen Winkel verborgen wird.
Hentzi war der kaiserliche General, der im Jahre
1849 die Festung Ofen gegen die Revolutions
truppen Kossuths unter deren Führer Görgey
bis zum letzten Blutstropfen verteidigte. Der
General, der, nebenbei bemerkt, von Geburt ein
Schweizer war, starb mit seiner kaiserlichen
Mannschaft den Heldentod, während Görgey die
Ofner Festung erstürmte. Im Jahre 1852
ließ Kaiser Franz Josef, als Ungarn ihm
gefesselt zu Füßen lag, zum Andenken an
den für ihn gefallenen Helden auf dem schönsten
Platze der Ofner Festung eine Statue errichten.
Dieses Denkmal war den Ungarn bis heute ein
wahrer Dorn im Auge. Vor etwa zehn Jahren
wurde sogar der Versuch gemacht, das Heutzi
denkmal durch eine Dynamitbombe in die Luft
zu sprengen. Als darauf der kaiserliche General
Joncsy an der Denkmalstätte eine Ansprache an
die Offiziere hielt und den gefallenen Helden als
ein Muster der Treue für den Kaiser feierte, kam
es fast zu einem Aufstande in Ungarn, das sich
in seinen Erinnerungen an die Kossuthsche Re
volution beleidigt fühlte. Nunmehr ergreift der
„König" Franz Josef selbst den Anlaß der
monumentalen Verherrlichung der gemordeten
Kaiserin, um Pest von dem verhaßten Denkmal
des Generals Hentzi zu befreien.
Der schwärmerische Dichter-Politiker Maurus
Jokai feiert das Ereignis in seinem Blatte,
indem er sagt, die Königin Elisabeth sei noch
nach ihrem Tode der Schutzengel Ungarns",
der der Nation zur Erfüllung eines lange ge
hegten Herzenswunsches verhelfe. Die Kossuth
partei faßt die Sache drastischer auf. Sie dankt
dem „König", für einen Entschluß, der einer
Stimmung Rechnung trug, die von der „Unab
hängigkeitspartei" vertreten wurde, während sie
jetzt durch die Regierung verwirklicht wird.
Wer waren die Truppen Görgeys, unter deren
Schüssen General Hentzi und seine Tapferen ver
bluteten? Es waren die Truppen des „Gouver
neurs" Kossuth und des Debrecziner Landtags,
der den Kaiser Franz Joseph und die Dynastie
Habsburg des ungarischen Thrones für verlustig
erklärt hatte. Welcher Wandel der Dinge, daß
heute derselbe „König von Ungarn" das Hentzi
denkmal entfernt, der es einst in Dankbarkeit für
die Heldentreue seines Generals hatte errichten
lassen! Aber die Obstruktion im Reichstage hält
trotzdem noch immer an. Jetzt wollen sie auch
noch die Trennung des Zollgebietes . ..
